16S rRNA amplicon profiling

Primers amplify a selected region of the 16S rRNA gene from sample DNA. Conserved stretches support primer binding; sequence variation within the amplified region helps distinguish some taxa. Results depend on primers, read quality, denoising, and reference database. Different taxa can share a marker sequence, so species-level labels are not always resolvable.

DADA2 models sequencing errors to infer amplicon sequence variants (ASVs). An ASV is an inferred sequence variant after denoising, not proof that each sequence represents a distinct organism or species. Historical OTU workflows cluster reads by a chosen similarity threshold; 97% is not a universal species boundary. Record method and parameters when comparing studies.

A complete QIIME 2 paired-end 16S workflow

In a full QIIME 2 amplicon workflow (Bolyen et al., 2019), demultiplexed paired-end FASTQ files are imported via a tab-separated manifest, inspected for per-cycle quality decay, trimmed of 5' PCR primers (qiime cutadapt trim-paired) if primers are still present in the reads, denoised into exact ASVs with DADA2 (Callahan et al., 2016), and then taxonomically classified against a region-matched reference database (SILVA 138 or Greengenes2):

# 1. Import demultiplexed paired-end FASTQs from a manifest TSV and summarize read quality
qiime tools import \
  --type 'SampleData[PairedEndSequencesWithQuality]' \
  --input-path pe-33-manifest.tsv \
  --output-path demux.qza \
  --input-format PairedEndFastqManifestPhred33V2

qiime demux summarize \
  --i-data demux.qza \
  --o-visualization demux-summary.qzv

# 2. Denoise, merge mates, and remove chimeras (adjust trunc-len from demux-summary.qzv!)
qiime dada2 denoise-paired \
  --i-demultiplexed-seqs demux.qza \
  --p-trunc-len-f 240 \
  --p-trunc-len-r 200 \
  --o-table table.qza \
  --o-representative-sequences rep-seqs.qza \
  --o-denoising-stats denoising-stats.qza

qiime metadata tabulate \
  --m-input-file denoising-stats.qza \
  --o-visualization denoising-stats.qzv

# 3. Assign taxonomy and filter host/organelle 16S contaminants (mitochondria, chloroplast)
qiime feature-classifier classify-sklearn \
  --i-classifier silva-138-99-nb-classifier.qza \
  --i-reads rep-seqs.qza \
  --o-classification taxonomy.qza

qiime taxa filter-table \
  --i-table table.qza \
  --i-taxonomy taxonomy.qza \
  --p-exclude mitochondria,chloroplast \
  --o-filtered-table table-no-organelle.qza

How to diagnose read loss in denoising-stats.qzv

Never treat table.qza creation as success without reading denoising-stats.qzv column by column: (1) a steep drop from input to filtered means --p-trunc-len-f/r extended into low-quality 3' bases so expected errors (maxEE) exceeded threshold; (2) a steep drop from denoised to merged means trunc_len_f + trunc_len_r < amplicon_length + 12 nt (for example, a ~460 bp V3-V4 amplicon requires >= 472 total retained bases to overlap by DADA2's 12 nt minimum); (3) losing > 25% of reads between merged and non-chimeric usually indicates unremoved 5' degenerate PCR primers, so run qiime cutadapt trim-paired before denoise-paired.

Annotating an assembled bacterial genome with Prokka and Bakta

Prokka (Seemann, 2014) predicts coding sequences (Prodigal), rRNAs (Barrnap), tRNAs (ARAGORN), and non-coding RNAs on assembled bacterial or archaeal contigs. Start with a quality-checked genome assembly (CheckM2 completeness/contamination and QUAST contiguity), never raw reads or 16S ASVs. Because Prokka is no longer actively updated upstream, its author recommends Bakta (Schwengers et al., 2021) for new bacterial annotation pipelines, particularly when standardized NCBI AMR/plasmid gene nomenclature (amrfinderplus, UniRef/RefSeq non-redundant protein clusters, and small-ORF detection) is needed.

Installation, contig-header preflight, and annotation runs

Always include conda-forge alongside bioconda so Perl/BLAST/HMMER dependencies resolve cleanly, and record exact software and database versions:

conda create -n genome-annot -c conda-forge -c bioconda prokka bakta
conda activate genome-annot
prokka --version
prokka --listdb

Before running Prokka on a SPAdes or Unicycler assembly (assembled_contigs.fasta), check two structural rules: first, no FASTA header may be empty; second, Prokka halts with [Error] Contig ID must be <= 37 chars long whenever assembler headers such as NODE_1_length_418920_cov_42.318541 exceed NCBI GenBank's 37-character locus limit. Pass --centre X --compliant so Prokka renames contigs cleanly during GenBank/GFF3 generation:

test -s assembled_contigs.fasta && grep -q '^>' assembled_contigs.fasta && ! grep -q '^>[[:space:]]*$' assembled_contigs.fasta && echo "FASTA headers non-empty"
# Prokka run (--compliant --centre X resolves long SPAdes contig headers)
prokka --outdir my_annotation --prefix isolate_01 --centre X --compliant --cpus 4 assembled_contigs.fasta

# Modern alternative: Bakta standardized bacterial genome annotation (requires downloaded bakta-db)
bakta --db /path/to/bakta-db --output bakta_isolate_01 --prefix isolate_01 --threads 4 assembled_contigs.fasta

On a completed run, confirm that my_annotation/isolate_01.gff, my_annotation/isolate_01.txt, and my_annotation/isolate_01.log exist, then inspect the log for a completion summary and the text summary for feature counts. Missing files, a non-zero exit status, or database/setup errors mean stop and resolve the failure before interpreting annotations. Counts are run-specific; there is no universal expected feature count. Output files do not validate the assembly or biological interpretation.

A QIIME 2 paired-read example

This command expects an existing QIIME 2 artifact of type SampleData[PairedEndSequencesWithQuality], already demultiplexed by sample; it does not import FASTQ files or create sample metadata. Inspect the artifact with qiime tools peek demux.qza and view per-cycle quality with qiime demux summarize --i-data demux.qza --o-visualization demux-summary.qzv, then open it with qiime tools view demux-summary.qzv. Choose truncation lengths from those plots and the target region, retaining sufficient paired-read overlap. The example produces a frequency table, representative sequences, and denoising statistics; compare input and retained read counts rather than treating file creation as success.

qiime dada2 denoise-paired \
  --i-demultiplexed-seqs demux.qza \
  --p-trunc-len-f 250 \
  --p-trunc-len-r 250 \
  --o-table table.qza \
  --o-representative-sequences rep-seqs.qza \
  --o-denoising-stats denoising-stats.qza

Do not copy 250 as a universal setting. Truncation removes 3′ bases and discards reads shorter than the selected length. Paired reads must retain sufficient overlap to merge; the documented default minimum is 12 nt. Poor choices can discard reads or prevent merging. Review quality plots and denoising statistics. Taxonomy assignment is separate and needs a reference compatible with the amplified region and classifier.

Start with an assembled genome in FASTA format, not raw reads, a feature table, or a 16S-only amplicon. Assembly contamination, fragmentation, and incorrect taxonomic or genetic-code assumptions can affect predictions and labels.

Prokka's maintainer now recommends considering Bakta for new pipelines because Prokka is no longer maintained. These commands explain the existing Prokka workflow; check maintenance and database status before choosing it for new production work.

Limitations, version & reference-data caveats, and responsible use

  • Package versions matter: plotting functions and defaults can change between versions. Save the package versions used with sessionInfo() inside a results/session_info.txt file to aid reproducibility.
  • Visualization does not substitute for statistical testing. For multi-donor condition differential expression, aggregate raw counts to sample-by-cell-type pseudobulks and test with DESeq2, edgeR, or limma-voom rather than treating pooled cells as independent replicates (Squair et al., 2021; see Differential Expression). For differential cell-type proportions across patients, use compositional models such as propeller (speckle), scCODA, or neighborhood-level miloR.
  • Color choices: Even colorblind-friendly palettes can fail for readers with other visual impairments. Provide clear legends, shape encodings, and high contrast. Include figure captions that explicitly describe color meaning and any transformation (for example, row z-score vs unscaled log-normalized values, or per-feature max scaling).
  • Data provenance: For multi-sample comparisons, ensure the object accounts for batch correction where needed. Visual patterns dominated by a single batch may reflect technical artifact rather than biology.

Troubleshooting

  • Output directory already exists: choose a new run name. Do not delete prior evidence just to make a rerun pass.
  • Counts rejected: check for missing fields, duplicate identifiers, non-integer values, or negative counts. Confirm you exported raw counts, not transformed expression.
  • Sample mismatch: compare identifiers exactly. Reordering metadata is allowed; inventing or silently dropping samples is not.
  • Zero-library normalization failure: inspect the original data and QC warning. Do not add artificial counts merely to bypass the check.
  • Optional provider failure: verify the SDK, model ID, account access, environment configuration, and schema support. Return to a clearly labeled offline run rather than silently treating it as AI output.

Practice with an observable result

  1. Reorder the three metadata rows in a copy. Rerun QC into a new directory. Sample identities and metrics should remain the same.
  2. In the Python CLI route, create a plan file containing {"steps":["qc","run_shell"]} and supply it with --plan blocked-plan.json. The plan must be rejected before tool execution.
  3. Add a duplicate gene or a fractional count to a copied input. Explain which validator rejects it and why silently coercing the value would be unsafe.
  4. Compare two offline runs of unchanged inputs. Match their hashes and numerical outputs; distinguish reproducibility of computation from validity of interpretation.

Check your understanding

Why can QC succeed when S3 has zero counts? Computing and flagging the zero total is valid; normalizing by that total is not. Does a valid model plan establish scientific correctness? No. It establishes only that the proposed tool sequence satisfies the local contract. What is the human approval point? Reviewing the evidence before using or reporting an analysis conclusion; the script never declares that approval on your behalf.

When descriptive CPM suffices vs when TMM or DESeq2 normalization is required

Dividing each gene's raw count by the sample's column sum (CPM) adjusts for sequencing depth only when overall transcriptome composition is stable across samples. In real RNA-seq cohorts, composition bias frequently violates that assumption: if a handful of hyper-abundant transcripts (such as immunoglobulin heavy/light chains in plasma-cell-infiltrated biopsies, haemoglobin in blood, or residual rRNA) consume 35% of sequencing reads in one condition, every genuinely unchanged gene in that library receives 35% fewer reads and appears artificially downregulated under simple CPM. Match your normalization and QC follow-up to the biological task:

  • Descriptive expression filtering and exploratory log-CPM plots: edgeR::cpm(y, log = TRUE) is useful after computing trimmed mean of M-values (calcNormFactors(y, method = "TMM"); Robinson & Oshlack, 2010) so effective library sizes resist composition skew.
  • Differential expression testing across biological replicates: pass unnormalized integer counts directly to DESeq2 (median-of-ratios size factors; Love et al., 2014) or edgeR quasi-likelihood negative-binomial GLMs (Robinson et al., 2010), never pre-computed CPM tables.
  • Investigating a flagged zero- or ultra-low-count sample (S3 = 0): before excluding a sample, check four upstream checkpoints: (1) demultiplexing barcode swap or empty library prep (FastQC read count), (2) reference build or chromosome-naming mismatch (STAR Log.final.out % Unmapped), (3) Ensembl-vs-symbol identifier mismatch (featureCounts .summary Unassigned_NoFeatures), or (4) wrong strand flag (-s 1 vs -s 2 verified with RSeQC infer_experiment.py, which drops ~95% of stranded reads when inverted).

References and further learning

  • Robinson, M. D., & Oshlack, A. (2010). A scaling normalization method for differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data (TMM). Genome Biology, 11, R25. doi:10.1186/gb-2010-11-3-r25
  • Robinson, M. D., McCarthy, D. J., & Smyth, G. K. (2010). edgeR: a Bioconductor package for differential expression analysis of digital gene expression data. Bioinformatics, 26(1), 139-140. doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btp616
  • Love, M. I., Huber, W., & Anders, S. (2014). Moderated estimation of fold change and dispersion for RNA-seq data with DESeq2. Genome Biology, 15, 550. doi:10.1186/s13059-014-0550-8

print(f"PASS: {n} paired records; normalized identifiers match in order" if n else "PASS: both files are empty") PY

A PASS establishes only that the parsed records have matching normalized identifiers in order under the stated convention; it does not establish sample identity or biological validity. Any malformed record, count difference, or identifier mismatch stops the check with the first location to investigate. Both small checks assume readable gzip inputs and ordinary first-token identifiers; adapt the opener for uncompressed FASTQ. They are not full FASTQ specification or compression-integrity validators. Do not treat quality scores as comparable across files until the encoding and instrument/pipeline provenance are known.

Check alignments, variants, and coordinate conventions

SAM/BAM/CRAM: headers, bitwise FLAGs, CIGAR strings, and reference lookup

# Header metadata, including @SQ sequence dictionary and @RG read groups
samtools view -H aligned.bam | sed -n '1,40p'

# Lightweight truncation check, followed by alignment-flag summaries
samtools quickcheck aligned.bam && echo "quickcheck passed" || echo "quickcheck failed"
samtools flagstat aligned.bam | sed -n '1,10p'

# For reference-compressed CRAM files, supply the exact reference FASTA via -T (or REF_PATH):
samtools view -T reference.fa -H sample.cram | head -n 20

Compare every @SQ contig name and length (LN:) with your reference .fai index, and verify @RG read-group SM: sample tags before variant calling. Below is one annotated SAM record illustrating the 11 mandatory tab-separated fields (Li et al., 2009):

read_042	99	chr17	7674220	60	10S140M	=	7674410	330	ACGT...	IIII...	NM:i:1	RG:Z:S01
  • FLAG = 99 (1 + 2 + 32 + 64): read is paired (1), mapped in a proper pair (2), mate is on the reverse strand (32), and this is read 1 (64; its reverse-strand mate carries FLAG = 147). Run samtools flags 99 anytime to decode bitwise flags without memorizing sums.
  • POS = 7674220 and MAPQ = 60: 1-based leftmost aligned reference base on chr17, with Phred-scaled mapping-uniqueness score 60 (note: in STAR RNA-seq BAMs, 255 denotes a unique mapper rather than unavailable MAPQ).
  • CIGAR = 10S140M: the first 10 bases at the 5' end were soft-clipped (10S, retained in SEQ because of unaligned adapter or overhang) followed by 140 aligned bases (140M, which include both sequence matches and single-base mismatches; inspect NM:i:1 or MD for exact mismatches).

VCF/BCF: header definitions, -H body records, and genotype fields

# Print ## meta-information header lines, then inspect the first 10 variant records (-H skips header!)
bcftools view -h variants.vcf.gz | sed -n '1,80p'
bcftools view -H variants.vcf.gz | head -n 10

# Summarize records; index statistics require a BGZF (.vcf.gz) + .tbi/.csi index
bcftools stats variants.vcf.gz | sed -n '1,40p'
bcftools index --stats variants.vcf.gz

Notice bcftools view -H (--no-header): running bcftools view variants.vcf.gz | sed -n '1,10p' without -H prints only the first ten ##contig or ##INFO header lines rather than variant rows. Each VCF body row is 1-based and carries sample-level allele evidence in FORMAT + sample columns:

chr17	7674220	.	C	T	1420.4	PASS	DP=82;AF=0.5	GT:AD:DP:GQ	0/1:44,38:82:99

Here 0/1 is an unphased heterozygous genotype (0|1 when phased), AD = 44,38 records 44 reference (C) reads and 38 alternate (T) reads (VAF = 38 / 82 = 0.463), DP = 82 is sample filtered read depth, and GQ = 99 is genotype Phred confidence.

Coordinate trap: 0-based half-open BED vs 1-based closed VCF and GTF

Off-by-one errors happen whenever BED intervals are mixed carelessly with VCF or GTF coordinates. For the single nucleotide at chr17 position 7,674,220 (*TP53* coding SNV):

  • 1-based closed (VCF, GTF/GFF3, SAM POS, IGV locus box): start = 7674220, end = 7674220 (length = end - start + 1 = 1).
  • 0-based half-open (BED, BAM binary pos, Python slicing): chromStart = 7674219, chromEnd = 7674220 (length = chromEnd - chromStart = 1). Convert with bedtools or bcftools -R targets.bed (which already knows .bed is 0-based!) rather than subtracting 1 ad hoc in spreadsheets.

Read annotations and count matrices (bulk and single-cell 10x MTX)

GTF/GFF: feature columns and coordinates

head -n 20 annotation.gtf
awk -F'\t' '$0 !~ /^#/ {print $3}' annotation.gtf | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 15

GTF/GFF feature lines have nine tab-separated fields; skipping # directive headers in awk ensures feature-type counts reflect real annotations (exon, CDS, transcript, gene). Confirm whether contig names use chr1 (GENCODE/UCSC) or 1 (Ensembl) before running STAR or featureCounts.

Count matrices and 10x sparse directories (matrix.mtx.gz / h5ad)

# Inspect a bulk TSV count matrix header and column count
head -n 6 counts.tsv
awk -F '\t' 'NR==1 {print; print "Columns:", NF}' counts.tsv

# Inspect a 10x Genomics sparse Matrix Market directory (barcodes = columns, features = rows)
zcat filtered_feature_bc_matrix/matrix.mtx.gz | head -n 5
zcat filtered_feature_bc_matrix/features.tsv.gz | head -n 3
zcat filtered_feature_bc_matrix/barcodes.tsv.gz | head -n 3

In a 10x Genomics Market Exchange directory, line 3 of matrix.mtx.gz prints n_features n_barcodes n_nonzero_entries; verify that n_features equals the line count of features.tsv.gz and n_barcodes equals barcodes.tsv.gz (note that Python AnnData / .h5ad transposes this convention to cells x genes, i.e., n_obs x n_vars). For bulk RNA-seq tables, fractional numbers are not always normalized expression: probabilistic transcript quantifiers (Salmon, kallisto, RSEM) output legitimate fractional estimated counts from multi-mapping expectation-maximization. Import them into DESeq2 or edgeR via tximport / tximeta (Soneson et al., 2015) with transcript-length offsets rather than rounding them manually or treating them as TPM.

Use failures to narrow the diagnosis

  • FASTQ line remainder, decompression error, or exit 141 under pipefail: test stream integrity with gzip -t reads_R1.fastq.gz. Note that under set -o pipefail, piping zcat large.fastq.gz | head -n 12 causes head to close the pipe early so zcat receives SIGPIPE (exit status 141); run full-stream checks with gzip -t rather than mistaking SIGPIPE on a preview for corruption.
  • Contigs missing during region extraction or CRAM decode failure: compare BAM @SQ names and lengths with the FASTA .fai index, and pass -T reference.fa when decoding CRAM files whose MD5 reference cache is offline.
  • VCF fields rejected or samples absent: inspect bcftools view -h and sample columns (bcftools query -l variants.vcf.gz) before filtering.
  • Decimal values in a count table: distinguish normalized values (TPM/FPKM/log-CPM, which must not be fed to count GLMs) from Salmon/kallisto expected counts (which belong in tximport).

What a successful check does not establish

File parsers and summary commands detect selected structural problems. They do not establish that files belong to the same sample, reference build, assay, or experimental design. Keep a sample sheet with explicit sample IDs and file paths; record reference and annotation releases, tool versions, checksums, and the commands used.

A PASS establishes only that the parsed records have matching normalized identifiers in order under the stated convention; it does not establish sample identity or biological validity. Any malformed record, count difference, or identifier mismatch stops the check with the first location to investigate. Both small checks assume readable gzip inputs and ordinary first-token identifiers; adapt the opener for uncompressed FASTQ. They are not full FASTQ specification or compression-integrity validators. Do not treat quality scores as comparable across files until the encoding and instrument/pipeline provenance are known.

Check alignments and variants against their references

SAM/BAM/CRAM: headers and file integrity

# Header metadata, including @SQ sequence dictionary and @RG read groups
samtools view -H aligned.bam | sed -n '1,40p'

# Lightweight truncation check, followed by alignment-flag summaries
samtools quickcheck aligned.bam && echo "quickcheck passed" || echo "quickcheck failed"
samtools flagstat aligned.bam | sed -n '1,10p'

Compare each @SQ sequence name and length with the intended reference, and check that read-group/sample identifiers agree with your sample sheet. quickcheck examines the header and file ending; it does not read the whole alignment body, so it can miss internal corruption. flagstat reads all records and reports flag-based categories. A mapping percentage is a diagnostic to investigate, not a universal pass/fail threshold or proof of alignment quality.

VCF/BCF: definitions, samples, and indexing

# Print metadata header and a small record sample
bcftools view -h variants.vcf.gz | sed -n '1,80p'
bcftools view variants.vcf.gz | sed -n '1,10p'

# Summarize records; index statistics require a usable index
bcftools stats variants.vcf.gz | sed -n '1,40p'
bcftools index --stats variants.vcf.gz

Read the ## metadata and final #CHROM header line. Check sample names, declared INFO/FORMAT fields such as DP or AD, and any reference/build information. Confirm REF alleles against the exact reference used by the calling workflow. A syntactically accepted VCF does not prove a variant is real; provenance, caller-specific filters, and appropriate validation still matter.

bcftools index --stats reads an existing index and reports per-contig record counts; it is not itself an integrity test. If no index is available, create one only when you intend to write a sidecar, for example bcftools index variants.vcf.gz for a BGZF-compressed VCF.

Read annotations and count tables

GTF/GFF: feature columns and coordinates

head -n 20 annotation.gtf
cut -f3 annotation.gtf | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | sed -n '1,20p'

GTF/GFF feature lines have nine tab-separated fields; column 3 is the feature type and column 9 carries attributes. GTF and GFF3 have distinct attribute conventions, so inspect the file's declared version and use a parser that matches it. Their feature coordinates are generally 1-based and inclusive; convert carefully when passing intervals to software using zero-based, half-open coordinates. Confirm sequence names against the reference. The cut example assumes records are tab-delimited and that comment/directive lines do not need special handling.

Count matrix: dimensions, identifiers, and value scale

# Inspect the header and a few rows
head -n 6 counts.tsv

# Show the first row and number of tab-delimited fields
awk -F '\t' 'NR==1 {print; print "Columns:", NF}' counts.tsv

Establish whether rows are genes, transcripts, or other features, and whether columns map to samples in a separate sample sheet. Find out whether values are raw counts, normalized abundance, or transformed measurements from the quantification method and its documentation. Integer-looking values alone do not establish that a matrix contains raw counts. Methods that model raw counts, including common differential-expression workflows, should not be given normalized or log-transformed values as if they were raw counts.

Use failures to narrow the diagnosis

  • FASTQ line remainder or decompression error: test the gzip stream with gzip -t reads_R1.fastq.gz, verify transfer checksums, and use a FASTQ-aware validator. Recover an intact source where possible; do not silently repair records based only on line counts.
  • Contigs missing during region extraction: compare BAM @SQ names and lengths with the FASTA index. A chr prefix difference can be a naming mismatch, while different lengths can signal a different assembly. Resolve provenance before renaming or realigning.
  • VCF fields rejected or samples absent: inspect the header and sample columns, then compare with the producing caller's documentation and logs. Reconstructing or editing a header without provenance can mislabel data.
  • Decimal values in a count table: determine whether the values are normalized or transformed and retrieve raw quantifier output if a count-based method requires it. Do not round normalized measurements to manufacture counts.

What a successful check does not establish

File parsers and summary commands detect selected structural problems. They do not establish that files belong to the same sample, reference build, assay, or experimental design. Keep a sample sheet with explicit sample IDs and file paths; record reference and annotation releases, tool versions, checksums, and the commands used. These checks do not replace statistical QC, assessment of biological replication, or independent validation of findings.

2. Run LIANA, understand its component scores, and plot top candidates

By default, R LIANA's liana_wrap() executes five distinct scoring frameworks against the OmniPath consensus ligand-receptor resource (natmi, connectome, logfc, SingleCellSignalR sca, and permutation-based cellphonedb) and combines their ranks with Robust Rank Aggregation in liana_aggregate() (Dimitrov et al., 2022).   • Specificity scores (such as natmi.edge_specificity, logfc.logfc_comb, and cellphonedb.pvalue) ask whether a ligand-receptor pair is enriched in a given sender-receiver pair relative to all other cell clusters in the dataset.
  • Expression magnitude scores (such as sca.LRscore and connectome.weight_sc) measure how strongly the ligand and receptor are expressed in the sender and receiver clusters, even when many other clusters express the same genes.

3. Multi-sample cohorts and when CellChat adds distinct value

Pooling cells across treatment arms or responders vs non-responders into two separate liana_wrap() calls treats cells as replicates and confounds shifts in donor composition with altered signaling. For multi-patient cohorts (for example pre- vs on-therapy tumour biopsies), keep biological replicates intact using one of two sample-aware strategies:

  • Sample-level LIANA + tensor decomposition: run liana_bysample() across donor IDs and decompose the four-way tensor (samples x senders x receivers x ligand-receptor pairs) with Tensor-cell2cell in the LIANA+ framework (Dimitrov et al., 2024) to identify communication programs that covary with patient condition.
  • Pseudobulk differential ligand-receptor and target modeling: use MultiNicheNet (Browaeys et al., 2023), which combines sample-level pseudobulk differential expression (edgeR) of ligands and receptors with downstream target-gene enrichment in receiver cells.

CellChat (Jin et al., 2021) models group-level communication probabilities using mass-action kinetics, agonist/antagonist cofactors, and curated pathway-level aggregation. It is complementary to LIANA rather than an independent validation step: because both read the same RNA expression matrix and overlapping literature databases, agreement between LIANA and CellChat prioritizes a transcriptomic hypothesis without proving physical protein contact. Follow the official CellChat repository and its Nature Protocols workflow when pathway-level network summaries are needed.

Interpret candidates, not causal messages

  • Ask whether a candidate is supported by multiple LIANA methods and whether source/target populations have adequate cells and plausible expression of the relevant ligand/receptor complex.

6. Bioinformatics file-naming rules and shell globbing (*, ?)

Consistent file naming makes cohorts scriptable and prevents silent sample mix-ups:

  • Never use spaces, parentheses, or slashes in filenames: an unquoted path such as Patient 1 (Tumour)_R1.fastq.gz splits on spaces into multiple shell arguments and breaks loops. Restrict names to ASCII letters, digits, underscores, hyphens, and dots, use zero-padded IDs (P01, P02, ..., P10) and ISO dates (2026-11-18) so alphabetical order matches numerical and chronological order, and never rename raw core-facility FASTQs without recording their original names and SHA-256 checksums in a sample sheet (see Reproducible Project Structure).
  • Preview shell globs with ls or echo before running a command that modifies files: in Bash and Zsh, * matches zero or more characters and ? matches exactly one character:
# Preview read-1 files only across a cohort directory before looping or moving
ls -lh projects/basic-nav/data/raw/*_R1.fastq.gz
echo projects/basic-nav/data/raw/sample_R?.fastq.gz

Four shell traps that destroy bioinformatics data: (1) typing > instead of >> immediately truncates an existing output file to 0 bytes before the command even starts; (2) spaces around a wildcard in rm * .tmp delete every file in the current directory instead of *.tmp; (3) on default case-insensitive macOS filesystems (APFS), writing tp53.tsv overwrites TP53.tsv whereas Linux ext4/XFS treats them as two distinct files; (4) copying a directory recursively into a subdirectory of itself creates nested copies.

Quick AWK primer before steps 5 to 7

Steps 5, 6, and 7 use awk, a streaming field-oriented processor that reads input one line (record) at a time and runs rules of the form pattern { action }:

  • Fields and delimiters: -F'\t' splits each line strictly on tabs rather than arbitrary whitespace; $0 is the whole line, $1 is column 1, $3 is column 3, and $NF is the last column on the line.
  • Line counters: NR is the cumulative line number across inputs (NR > 1 skips a single-line header; NR % 4 == 1 matches lines 1, 5, 9, ...).
  • Associative arrays for exact joins: in awk -F'\t' 'FILENAME == ARGV[1] {a[$1]=1; next} ($1 in a)' ids.txt data.tsv, the first pass stores every ID from ids.txt as a hash key in a, and the second pass prints rows of data.tsv whose column 1 matches an exact key in a in linear time.

A channel is a repository of package metadata and package archives. For many bioinformatics workflows, conda-forge provides general dependencies and bioconda provides many domain-specific tools. Channel configuration affects the solver, so keep it explicit and avoid mixing unrelated defaults without understanding the consequences.

For this lesson, keep channel choices on each command instead of changing a shared .condarc/.mambarc. Bioconda recommends conda-forge before bioconda on the command line (higher priority first) and strict priority. Each create command below therefore uses both --override-channels and --channel-priority strict: the first prevents configured default channels from silently joining the solve, while the second enforces the declared order. In particular, do not add Anaconda defaults implicitly.

micromamba create -n qc-demo-channels \
  --override-channels -c conda-forge -c bioconda --channel-priority strict \
  fastqc multiqc

Include these options on every create command to make its channel selection independent of machine-level channel configuration. micromamba config list and micromamba info are useful for inspecting configured values, but --override-channels governs these invocations. Strict priority constrains solver choices; it cannot make unavailable packages or unsupported platforms work.

When a package cannot be solved, first check its availability, platform support, channel choice, and version constraints. Do not immediately add many channels or remove all version pins; that can create a solution that is difficult to reproduce.

micromamba create -n qc-demo-basic \
  --override-channels -c conda-forge -c bioconda --channel-priority strict \
  python=3.11 fastqc multiqc

# Activate it in the current shell
micromamba activate qc-demo-basic

# Confirm which executable and Python are active
which python

UMAP: explore neighborhoods with a specified input

When not to use UMAP: UMAP is designed for large neighborhood graphs (such as thousands of cells in single-cell transcriptomics) and is not informative for small bulk cohorts (such as 6 to 20 RNA-seq samples), where PCA or MDS faithfully represents variance and global distances without non-linear distortion. The 6-sample UMAP block below exists strictly to teach the software mechanics, sample-alignment assertions, and n_neighbors < N guardrails before you encounter UMAP in single-cell workflows. A container can make a bioinformatics tool's software environment easier to reuse, but it does not package your reads, reference genome, scheduler policy, or every host dependency. This walkthrough traces file paths in a local Docker BWA-MEM example and an optional Apptainer/Slurm script, with attention to the files each command can actually see.

Format: Hands-on lab. For learners comfortable with a terminal, the local exercise creates a tiny, entirely synthetic reference and two reads, then follows their files through BWA in Docker. It requires a Docker-capable host (no host-side BWA installation is needed because both indexing and mapping run inside the container); no biological data are supplied. If Docker is unavailable, the file-flow check below can be completed without running commands. The Slurm/Apptainer section is an optional adaptation for users with an authorized cluster account.

What the container freezes, and what it does not

An image bundles an application and its userspace dependencies. That is useful when tools require conflicting libraries or when you need to preserve an environment, but it does not guarantee identical results across all hosts: kernel and hardware behavior, environment variables, mounted files, command-line parameters, and external services can still matter. Record the exact image reference (prefer an immutable @sha256:... digest for durable identification), input checksums, tool arguments, and relevant host/runtime details. A tag can be moved, and a container is not a substitute for workflow provenance or biological validation.

Docker commonly runs through a privileged daemon, which is why shared clusters restrict Docker. In 2021, the open-source Singularity project moved into the Linux Foundation and was renamed Apptainer, while Sylabs maintains SingularityCE separately; HPC documentation and module systems may expose either apptainer or singularity. Unlike Docker (which starts with an isolated filesystem and clean environment), Apptainer binds your host $HOME directory and inherits host environment variables (such as PYTHONPATH and R_LIBS_USER) by default, so pass --cleanenv (or --containall with explicit --bind) whenever host dotfiles conflict with libraries inside the container.

Prepare a small, explicit project layout

For a reproducible smoke test, create the fixture below in a new project directory. It is invented sequence data for checking file flow only, not a biological sample or a test of BWA's suitability for any assay. Both indexing and mapping run inside the same container image so no host BWA installation is needed, preventing index/mapper version drift. Check that Bash and Docker are available before starting:

command -v docker && docker --version

    • Pinning BioContainers images by digest and authoring minimal Dockerfiles

    For single command-line bioinformatics tools (bwa, samtools, bcftools, fastp, minimap2), prefer existing community-tested images from BioContainers (quay.io/biocontainers/..., automatically built from every Bioconda package release; da Veiga Leprevost et al., 2017) rather than maintaining ad hoc Dockerfiles. Because registry tags can be overwritten, resolve and record the immutable SHA-256 manifest digest after pulling:

    # Inspect the immutable OCI digest and run by @sha256 for long-term archival reproducibility
docker pull quay.io/biocontainers/bwa:0.7.17--hed695b0_7
docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' quay.io/biocontainers/bwa:0.7.17--hed695b0_7
# Example pinned reference format: quay.io/biocontainers/bwa@sha256:<64-hex-digest>

    When a project combines custom R or Python scripts that no single BioContainer bundles, keep the Dockerfile minimal, pin the base image version, and clean package caches in the same RUN layer:

    FROM rocker/r-ver:4.3.3
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libcurl4-openssl-dev libxml2-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN Rscript -e 'options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://packagemanager.posit.co/cran/2024-04-15")); install.packages(c("readr", "dplyr"))'
WORKDIR /work

    Choosing between Docker and Apptainer

    Use Docker where you control the host and its daemon is permitted; use Apptainer on an HPC system that supports it and documents the necessary execution policy. Both can run OCI-origin images, but runtime configuration, bind defaults ($HOME mounted automatically in Apptainer vs isolated by default in Docker), environment handling, and supported options differ. Workflow managers such as Snakemake (--sdm apptainer) and Nextflow (-profile singularity or -profile apptainer) automate per-step container execution across local and Slurm runs.

    • 4b) Optional alignment trimming (ClipKIT or trimAl) and when trimming hurts

    Divergent untranslated flanks or hypervariable loops can introduce non-homologous gap columns into a multiple sequence alignment, particularly in deep phylogenomic datasets. Modern alignment trimmers such as ClipKIT (Steenwyk et al., 2020, retaining parsimony-informative sites while excising gappy columns) or trimAl (-automated1 / -gt 0.8) provide reproducible column filtering:

    # Optional column trimming (check retained alignment length before and after!)
clipkit results/aligned_sequences.fasta -m smart-gap -o results/aligned_trimmed.fasta

    Do not trim reflexively on short single-locus alignments: Tan et al. (2015) demonstrated across large empirical benchmarks that aggressive automated trimming often removes genuine phylogenetic signal and degrades single-gene tree accuracy relative to untrimmed alignments. Always compare alignment column count before and after trimming, and compare tree topologies if more than 20 to 30% of sites are removed.

    5) Build a maximum-likelihood tree with IQ-TREE 2 (recommended CLI route)

    IQ-TREE 2 (Minh et al., 2020) integrates substitution-model selection (ModelFinder, Kalyaanamoorthy et al., 2017), tree search, ultrafast bootstrap approximation (UFBoot2, Hoang et al., 2018), and Shimodaira-Hasegawa approximate likelihood-ratio testing (SH-aLRT) in one reproducible command. Note the executable and option names across releases: IQ-TREE v1 used iqtree -bb 1000 -pre ..., whereas IQ-TREE v2/v3 uses iqtree2 (or iqtree3) with -B 1000 --prefix ...:

    # Select best-fit substitution model (-m MFP), compute 1,000 UFBoot2 (-B) and 1,000 SH-aLRT (-alrt) replicates.
# Optional: pass `-o OUTGROUP_TAXON_ID` matching an exact header ID in aligned_sequences.fasta to root the output display.
iqtree2 -s results/aligned_sequences.fasta -m MFP -B 1000 -alrt 1000 --prefix results/iqtree_run -T AUTO

# Record exact executable version for provenance
iqtree2 --version

    Key IQ-TREE outputs and how to read dual branch supports (SH-aLRT / UFBoot written at internal nodes in results/iqtree_run.treefile):

    • results/iqtree_run.iqtree: human-readable analysis report listing alignment sites, constant vs parsimony-informative sites, BIC-selected substitution model (for example GTR+F+I+G4 or LG+G4), log-likelihood, and an ASCII preview of the tree.
    • Interpreting UFBoot2 vs classic bootstrap: UFBoot2 (-B 1000) is not calibrated identically to Felsenstein's standard nonparametric bootstrap (-b 100). Whereas 70% is often treated as moderate support in standard bootstrapping, the IQ-TREE authors recommend requiring UFBoot >= 95% together with SH-aLRT >= 80% before calling a clade well supported under the fitted model (Minh et al., 2020).

With the fixture, each lane contains one control and one treated sample. Notice an instructive hidden flaw in the remaining columns, however: Lane1 contains only female donors (sex = F) collected on 2024-01-12, whereas Lane2 contains only male donors (sex = M) collected on 2024-01-13. Explore expression patterns with PCA

PCA can help reveal dominant patterns in an expression matrix, but it is exploratory and cannot label a pattern as biological or technical by itself. Choose either the base R or Python implementation below. Both require a finite, non-negative count matrix in counts.csv, with feature IDs in the first column and sample IDs as column names, plus the validated metadata produced by either validator. Counts columns must match metadata sample IDs exactly; each implementation aligns metadata to the count-column order. The log-CPM-like transform is a simple exploratory transform, not a count-model input for differential-expression testing.

Choose a modeling response

How to handle known batch variables by downstream task
Downstream goalRecommended approachWhy not substitute another matrix?
Differential expression on RNA-seq countsInclude batch directly in the count GLM design (for example ~ batch + condition in DESeq2, edgeR, or limma-voom).Preserves count mean-variance relationships and exact residual degrees of freedom; feeding batch-regressed continuous values into count models distorts dispersion and inflates false positives.
Exploratory PCA, clustering, or heatmapsCompute vst() or log2(CPM + 1), then apply limma::removeBatchEffect(mat, batch = meta$batch, design = model.matrix(~ condition, meta)) or sva::ComBat for display only.Unadjusted PCA can be visually dominated by lane/center shifts even when condition is well balanced, but the regressed matrix should never be passed back into DE testing.
Count-scale batch adjustment across studiesUse a negative-binomial count adjustment such as sva::ComBat_seq(counts, batch = meta$batch, group = meta$condition) when downstream tools strictly require integer counts.Still requires conditions to overlap across batches; cannot unconfound a batch that contains only one biological group.
  • Conditions represented across batches: include batch and condition in the analysis design when supported by the study structure. Paired, repeated-measures, interaction, or nested designs require terms (or random effects such as limma::duplicateCorrelation) that reflect those units.

Reproducible block randomization before library preparation

Prevent batch confounding before wet-lab processing by assigning samples to plates or lanes within condition strata using a recorded random seed:

set.seed(20261018)
samples <- data.frame(
  sample_id = sprintf("S%02d", 1:12),
  condition = rep(c("control", "treated"), each = 6)
)
# Assign equal numbers of control and treated samples to Plate1 and Plate2, then shuffle plate order
samples$plate <- ave(samples$condition, samples$condition, FUN = function(x) {
  sample(rep(c("Plate1", "Plate2"), length.out = length(x)))
})
samples <- samples[order(samples$plate, sample(seq_len(nrow(samples)))), ]
print(table(samples$plate, samples$condition))

A PCA colored by batch may show a strong technical pattern, but it does not prove all condition-associated differences are technical. Clustering by condition does not rule out batch effects either. Compare diagnostics, design structure, and model assumptions; report sensitivity analyses rather than presenting a corrected visualization as proof.

Choose a modeling response

  • Conditions represented across batches: include batch and condition in the analysis design when supported by the study structure. For a simple independent-sample RNA-seq comparison, a DESeq2 design might be ~ batch + condition; it is an example, not a universal formula. Paired, repeated-measures, interaction, or nested designs require terms that reflect those units and questions.
  • Perfect confounding or missing combinations: inspect the model matrix and resolve the design before data collection if possible. When the study is already complete and effects are not identifiable, report that limitation; removing a batch column from a formula makes an assumption, not a recovery of its effect.
  • Considering batch-adjusted expression for visualization or another downstream task: use a method appropriate for the data type and purpose, and include the biological variables whose signal must be protected as required by that method. For example, the sva package documents ComBat's model matrix for adjustment variables. Do not treat an adjusted matrix as a replacement for the count model used for differential-expression inference.

• The directives request resources: --ntasks is the number of processes/tasks and --cpus-per-task is CPUs per task. In the smoke test, one task times one CPU per task requests one CPU total; that script does not specify a memory amount. These are requests subject to site limits and scheduler configuration.

    Note: Allocating a lot of resources does not mean that all of them will be used. If a program is not configured for parallel execution, it will use one CPU even when more are allocated. Start with a documented estimate, run a small test, then inspect actual resource use with the scheduler rather than logging directly into a compute node:

    squeue -j JOB_ID                 # queue state while pending or running
sstat -j JOB_ID.batch --format=JobID,MaxRSS,AveCPU
sacct -j JOB_ID --format=JobID,State,Elapsed,MaxRSS,AllocCPUS

    If you need an interactive diagnostic session, request one through the scheduler, for example srun --pty --cpus-per-task=2 --mem=8G --time=01:00:00 bash. Only SSH to a compute node when your own cluster documentation explicitly permits it.

    Actual CPU allocation and binding can differ with the cluster's select and task plugins, core/thread topology, and request options. Check the local documentation and the allocation reported for your job rather than assuming a fixed multiplier.

Several independent steps in parallel (srun --exact)

In Slurm 20.11+, a background srun step without --exact can claim all CPUs or memory of the parent allocation and block subsequent background steps until the first step finishes. Pass --exact with explicit per-step --ntasks, --cpus-per-task, and --mem so all three 1-CPU / 2-GiB steps run concurrently inside the 3-CPU / 6-GiB job:

#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name example_script
#SBATCH --ntasks 3
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task 1
#SBATCH --mem 6G
#SBATCH --partition YOUR_ALLOWED_PARTITION
#SBATCH --output %x-%j.out

module purge
# module load REPLACE_WITH_SITE_MODULE

srun --exact --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=2G program0 &
step0_pid=$!
srun --exact --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=2G program1 &
step1_pid=$!
srun --exact --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=2G program2
step2_status=$?
wait "$step0_pid"
step0_status=$?

The shell records and waits for both background PIDs and checks the foreground step so any failed sub-step makes the batch job exit nonzero instead of silently masking an earlier crash.

Job arrays for multi-sample bioinformatics cohorts

For processing 10 or 100 independent FASTQ samples through the same aligner or variant caller, a Slurm job array is cleaner and safer than background subshells because each sample gets its own independent State, MaxRSS, and retryable array task ID (SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID):

#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name example_array
#SBATCH --array=0-2%2
#SBATCH --ntasks 1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task 1
#SBATCH --mem 2G
#SBATCH --partition YOUR_ALLOWED_PARTITION
#SBATCH --output %x-%A-%a.out

module purge
# module load REPLACE_WITH_SITE_MODULE

srun program --arg=$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

This array launches task indices 0, 1, and 2 with at most 2 running concurrently (%2, useful for avoiding filesystem I/O saturation), and %A / %a write separate logs per array master ID and task index. In real cohorts, map SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (1-based --array=1-N) to row N of a tab-separated samples.tsv manifest via awk -v idx="$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID" 'NR == idx {print $1}'.

Optional: running an interactive session

srun --pty --job-name interactive --partition YOUR_ALLOWED_PARTITION --mem 2G --cpus-per-task 1 bash

srun --pty requests an interactive shell on a compute node through Slurm rather than running heavy jobs on shared login nodes.

This is an optional advanced pattern, not a first-job script. Each step requests one task so each command runs once; the shell records and waits for both background process IDs and checks the foreground command too. Arrays

A job array is useful for independent repetitions of the same script with an index-specific input or argument. The index values need not be consecutive; make sure your script maps every requested index to a valid input and that tasks do not overwrite one another's files.

#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name example_script

#SBATCH --array=0-2

#SBATCH --ntasks 1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task 1
#SBATCH --mem 2G

#SBATCH --partition ibrain
#SBATCH --output %x-%A-%a.out
#SBATCH --hint=nomultithread


module purge
module load gcc/7.3.1

srun program --arg=$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

This array has task indices 0, 1, and 2. Slurm sets SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to each task's index; %A and %a make the log name unique per array and task. Before scaling up, test the index-to-input mapping for the first, last, and an invalid index, and consider a concurrency cap such as --array=0-2%2 if the site permits it. Array scheduling order is not guaranteed.

Optional: running an interactive session

srun --pty --job-name interactive --partition ibrain --mem 2G --cpus-per-task 1 bash

srun --pty requests an interactive pseudo-terminal through Slurm; it may wait until requested resources become available. The final bash is the command started in that allocation. Use only resources and partitions allowed by local policy. A graphical session requires additional site support; do not assume replacing Bash with an application is sufficient.

Optional advanced topic: running a GUI with X11

srun --pty --job-name gui --partition ibrain --mem 2G --cpus-per-task 1 --x11 bash

--x11 requests X11 forwarding, which requires Slurm and the cluster's configuration to support it as well as a working local display setup. This command is not portable to every cluster. Follow site instructions for graphical applications, or use a supported remote visualization service.

Optional advanced topic: custom modules

Creating a custom module

If you have a program you want to make available to others, you can create a custom module for it. This involves creating a module file that defines the environment variables and paths needed to run your program.

Example module file (myprogram/1.0.lua):

help([[This module loads MyProgram version 1.0]])

prepend_path("PATH", "/path/to/myprogram/bin")
prepend_path("LD_LIBRARY_PATH", "/path/to/myprogram/lib")

This is a site-administered environment-modules example, not a complete user setup. Module systems differ; ask the cluster administrator how user modulefiles are enabled. The module use command adds a directory to the module search path; it does not simply print MODULEPATH.

Using a custom module

Once your custom module is created and placed in the correct location, you can load it like any other module:

module load myprogram/1.0

Choose a format supported by the downstream tools and balance CPU time against storage savings. In genomics, distinguish standard single-stream gzip from bgzip (blocked GNU zip from htslib / samtools): standard gzip works for sequentially streamed FASTQ files, whereas indexed coordinate-sorted VCF (.vcf.gz + .tbi/.csi), BED, and FASTA files must be compressed with bgzip (bgzip variants.vcf && tabix -p vcf variants.vcf.gz) because tabix and bcftools index reject plain gzip streams.

    • Quantifying a per-cell CNV burden score against the diploid reference

    In addition to visual inspection of infercnv.png (where, for example, IDH-wildtype glioblastoma cohorts such as Darmanis et al. GSE84465 classically exhibit coordinated chromosome 7 gain paired with chromosome 10 loss in neoplastic cells while immune/vascular reference rows stay neutral), summarize each cell's genome-wide deviation from the neutral baseline in final_check@expr.data and compare observation groups against the reference distribution:

    # Compute per-cell mean-squared CNV deviation from the neutral baseline (typically 1.0)
expr_mat <- final_check@expr.data
neutral_center <- stats::median(expr_mat[, unlist(final_check@reference_grouped_cell_indices), drop = FALSE])
cnv_score <- colMeans((expr_mat - neutral_center)^2)

score_df <- data.frame(
  cell_id = names(cnv_score),
  cnv_msq = as.numeric(cnv_score),
  cell_type = annotations$cell_type[match(names(cnv_score), annotations$cell_id)],
  is_reference = annotations$cell_type[match(names(cnv_score), annotations$cell_id)] %in% reference_groups
)
# Compare candidate malignant clusters against the 95th/99th percentile of diploid reference cells
ref_q99 <- stats::quantile(score_df$cnv_msq[score_df$is_reference], probs = 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)
print(aggregate(cnv_msq ~ cell_type + is_reference, data = score_df, FUN = stats::median))
message("99th percentile of diploid reference CNV score: ", round(ref_q99, 5))

    A global CNV burden score flags high-aneuploidy clusters relative to internal normal cells, though diploid or near-diploid tumors (such as many acute leukemias or pediatric cancers driven by balanced translocations) will score near the reference distribution and require fusion, mutation, or allele-specific BAF callers (such as Numbat when BAMs are available).

    What a plausible positive result means:

    • Coordinated amplification or deletion across many genes in a contiguous genomic region is consistent with a copy-number lesion and can be used to prioritise cells/clusters for DNA validation.

Example command: what a BLASTP search requires

The following is a command pattern, not a bundled run: it assumes NCBI BLAST+ is installed and protein.fasta contains a valid amino-acid query. blastp -query protein.fasta -db swissprot -evalue 1e-5 \
  -outfmt "6 qseqid sseqid pident length mismatch gapopen qstart qend sstart send evalue bitscore qcovs" \
  -out results.tsv

# Option B: standard 12-column outfmt 6 against a pre-installed local database
blastp -query protein.fasta -db nr -evalue 1e-5 -out results.txt -outfmt 6

Replace the example paths and thread count. Kraken2 accepts compressed FASTQ input. With --paired, give the read-1 file followed by the corresponding read-2 file. Keep mates synchronized after preprocessing.

kraken2 --db /path/to/kraken2_database \
  --threads 16 \
  --confidence 0.05 \
  --paired sample_R1.fastq.gz sample_R2.fastq.gz \
  --report sample.kreport \
  --output sample.kraken

sample.kraken records each classified fragment, while sample.kreport aggregates counts by taxon. Notice --confidence 0.05: Kraken2's default is --confidence 0.0, under which a single diagnostic k-mer match on an otherwise uninformative or host-derived read can trigger a species call and generate long tails of 1- to 3-read false-positive taxa (a frequent pitfall in low-biomass clinical or intratumoural microbiome studies). Setting --confidence 0.05 or 0.10 requires that fraction of scored k-mers in the read pair to support the called clade, trading slightly lower species sensitivity for substantially fewer spurious hits (Wood et al., 2019).

2. Estimate abundance with Bracken

Use the same Kraken database and its matching Bracken k-mer distribution files (database150mers.kmer_distrib, etc.). Set -r to match your post-trimming read length and -t to the minimum read count required before Bracken re-estimates a taxon (-t 10 by default, preventing noisy redistribution onto single-read artifacts; Lu et al., 2017):

bracken -d /path/to/kraken2_database \
  -i sample.kreport \
  -o sample.bracken.S.tsv \
  -w sample.bracken.kreport \
  -r 150 \
  -l S \
  -t 10

Here -l S requests species-level estimates and -r 150 is only an example. Bracken redistributes some reads assigned higher in the taxonomy using a model derived from the database's expected read-length k-mer classifications. Its output distinguishes Kraken-assigned reads, added reads after re-estimation, total reads after re-estimation, and fraction of total. Those adjusted counts are model-based estimates, not newly observed species-specific reads.

Before trusting this run: confirm the Bracken distribution file exists for the selected read length and database, and inspect the output for errors. A missing or mismatched distribution file is a setup failure, not a reason to interpret raw Kraken counts as Bracken estimates.

3. Read the reports before making a biological claim

Start with the Kraken report's unclassified fraction and high-level assignments. Compare the Kraken direct and clade counts with the Bracken estimates at the chosen rank. Large unresolved fractions can reflect database coverage, sequence quality, or other pipeline factors; they do not identify a single cause. Unexpected taxa warrant checks of negative controls, database contents, host-read handling, and read quality before interpretation.

Database composition defines which sequences can be recognized and can also affect ambiguous assignments. Do not assume a standard database is adequate for every environment or that adding more references always improves a particular analysis. Document the database build and assess likely contaminants, especially when custom references are used.

Relative abundance describes the sequenced library after extraction, library preparation, sequencing, and classification. Biases in those steps can make it differ from the underlying community, and compositional proportions do not provide absolute abundance. Cross-sample comparisons require consistent processing and a clear rationale for normalization; cross-study comparisons add further differences in protocols and databases.

4. Convert reports safely for Krona hierarchical visualization

Do not pass a 6-column Kraken2 .kreport directly to generic ktImportText: convert either the Kraken2 report (sample.kreport) or Bracken's Kraken-style report (-w sample.bracken.kreport) into Krona's hierarchical tab-delimited format first using kreport2krona.py from KrakenTools (Lu et al., 2022):

# Convert Bracken's updated Kraken-style report (-w) to Krona text, then render HTML

  --paired sample_R1.fastq.gz sample_R2.fastq.gz \
  --report sample.kreport \

sample.kraken records each classified fragment, while sample.kreport aggregates counts by taxon. The report includes the percentage and fragment count for each taxon's subtree, direct-assignment count, rank code, taxid, and indented scientific name. A genus-level or higher assignment is an unresolved classification at that rank, not evidence that a specific species was detected. 2. Estimate abundance with Bracken

Use the same Kraken database and its matching Bracken distribution files. Set -r to the read length represented by the distribution files and appropriate for your processed reads, not automatically the sequencer's nominal length. If trimming leaves variable or shorter reads, consult Bracken guidance and choose a defensible representative length; record that choice. Choose the target rank deliberately.

bracken -d /path/to/kraken2_database \
  -i sample.kreport \
  -o sample.bracken.S.tsv \
  -r 150 \
  -l S

Here -l S requests species-level estimates and -r 150 is only an example. Bracken redistributes some reads assigned higher in the taxonomy using a model derived from the database's expected read-length k-mer classifications. Its output distinguishes Kraken-assigned reads, added reads after re-estimation, total reads after re-estimation, and fraction of total. Those adjusted counts are model-based estimates, not newly observed species-specific reads.

Before trusting this run: confirm the Bracken distribution file exists for the selected read length and database, and inspect the output for errors. A missing or mismatched distribution file is a setup failure, not a reason to interpret raw Kraken counts as Bracken estimates.

3. Read the reports before making a biological claim

Start with the Kraken report's unclassified fraction and high-level assignments. Compare the Kraken direct and clade counts with the Bracken estimates at the chosen rank. Large unresolved fractions can reflect database coverage, sequence quality, or other pipeline factors; they do not identify a single cause. Unexpected taxa warrant checks of negative controls, database contents, host-read handling, and read quality before interpretation.

Database composition defines which sequences can be recognized and can also affect ambiguous assignments. Do not assume a standard database is adequate for every environment or that adding more references always improves a particular analysis. Document the database build and assess likely contaminants, especially when custom references are used.

Relative abundance describes the sequenced library after extraction, library preparation, sequencing, and classification. Biases in those steps can make it differ from the underlying community, and compositional proportions do not provide absolute abundance. Cross-sample comparisons require consistent processing and a clear rationale for normalization; cross-study comparisons add further differences in protocols and databases.

4. Visualize only after choosing a compatible input

KronaTools has importers for supported input formats. Do not pass a Kraken report to the generic ktImportText command as though it were a two-column taxon/weight file: the Kraken report is a six-column hierarchical format. Select the importer and input format documented for your installed KronaTools version, or convert data explicitly to its documented text format. Bracken output is also not automatically interchangeable with every importer.

Visualization is out of scope here: no plot is produced because importer compatibility depends on KronaTools version and input representation. Consult the linked import guide, then validate any conversion on a small input and compare its totals with the source table before interpreting a plot.

4. Interpret the species tree and choose downstream analysis

In OrthoFinder 3.2, a standard core -f run infers its species tree from a concatenated alignment of single-copy orthogroups. The --assign workflow, or an explicit -ST astral-pro choice, uses gene-tree-based ASTRAL-Pro inference instead. Older releases and settings used STAG for species-tree inference and STRIDE for rooting from gene-duplication evidence. Record the actual release, workflow and tree options; do not describe every OrthoFinder run as STAG-based or as never using concatenation. The topology and root depend on the inputs, taxon sampling, available signal and settings. Treat the tree as an estimate to inspect, not a guaranteed true history.

For a separate phylogenomic analysis, aligned loci can be concatenated and analysed as a partitioned supermatrix, or gene trees can be estimated locus by locus and summarized with a coalescent method such as ASTRAL. for fa in OrthoFinder/Results_*/Single_Copy_Orthologue_Sequences/OG*.fa; do
  og=$(basename "$fa" .fa)
  mafft --auto "$fa" > "aligned_sco/${og}.aln.faa"
  clipkit "aligned_sco/${og}.aln.faa" -o "trimmed_sco/${og}.trim.faa"

iqtree2 -p trimmed_sco/ -m MFP -B 1000 -alrt 1000 -T AUTO --prefix sco_concat

Concatenation and coalescent summary methods (such as estimating one IQ-TREE gene tree per locus and summarizing with astral / astral-pro) answer complementary questions: concatenation pools weak per-gene signal across loci, whereas coalescent summaries accommodate incomplete lineage sorting (ILS) while inheriting individual gene-tree estimation error. Compare both topologies and inspect gene/site concordance factors (iqtree2 --gcf --scf) when key nodes disagree.

Use the exact results directory printed by your run. In OrthoFinder 3.1 or later, open Orthogroups/Orthogroups.tsv; a legacy run may instead use the documented root-level HOG table Phylogenetic_Hierarchical_Orthogroups/N0.tsv. For example, counts 1, 1, 1 across three species give three sequences and make that row an all-species single-copy candidate; 2, 1, 1 gives four sequences and is not single-copy. These are arithmetic examples, not claimed OrthoFinder output.

  1. Record the OrthoFinder version, species filenames, input sequence type and results path.
  2. Choose one orthogroup, transcribe its ID and per-species copy counts, and label it all-species single-copy only if every species contributes exactly one.
  3. Find the gene tree corresponding to that group using the filename/ID convention documented for your release. If no tree is provided for the group, report that absence rather than substituting another group's tree. Note missing taxa, multiplicity, weakly supported or long branches, and alignment concerns; a gene tree is not an alignment-quality assessment.

FastQC writes a report for each input file. MultiQC searches the supplied directory for recognized report files and compiles a combined report; review sample names and modules to ensure it found the intended inputs.

3. Trim only when a report supports it

By default, fastp enables quality filtering (Phred < 15 in >40% of bases), N-base filtering (>5 Ns), and minimum-length filtering (15 bp) in addition to adapter trimming; pass --disable_quality_filtering if you strictly want adapter-only removal. Retain the original FASTQ in raw/ and write trimmed reads and reports to separate paths:

set -euo pipefail
# Input: raw/*.fastq.gz
# Output: trimmed/sample_R1.trim.fastq.gz, trimmed/sample_R2.trim.fastq.gz
mkdir -p trimmed qc
fastp -i raw/sample_R1.fastq.gz -I raw/sample_R2.fastq.gz \
      -o trimmed/sample_R1.trim.fastq.gz -O trimmed/sample_R2.trim.fastq.gz \
      --detect_adapter_for_pe \
      --thread 4 --html qc/fastp_report.html --json qc/fastp_report.json

Note: adapt parameters to your platform and chemistry (for NovaSeq/NextSeq two-color instruments, consider --trim_poly_g). Keep qc/fastp_report.html and qc/fastp_report.json alongside MultiQC.

The indexing line writes companion files beside the FASTA and is needed only once for that exact reference and aligner version. Use a writable reference copy, or skip that line when matching bwa-mem2 indexes have already been prepared. A FASTA .fai alone is not a bwa-mem2 index.

What this QC can and cannot tell you

A per-sample sum can flag a possible library-size or data-import discrepancy. It does not establish why a sample differs, and total counts alone do not establish differential expression or other biological effects. Raw counts can be compared as a basic descriptive QC measure, but differential-expression workflows need appropriate normalization and statistical models that reflect the experiment and its variability. Do not use these totals as normalized expression values.

Note why the column is named total_counts_millions rather than RPM (reads per million) or CPM (counts per million): dividing a sample's sum of counts by 1e6 merely rescales the sample total into millions of counts, whereas RPM/CPM divides each individual gene's count by the sample library size and multiplies by one million so every sample sums to 1e6.

Core dplyr verbs on the joined gene-by-sample table

Once joined passes key and integer-count checks in scripts/01-tidy-qc.R, five core dplyr verbs handle most exploratory tabular transformations in bioinformatics: select() chooses columns, filter() subsets rows by logical predicates, group_by() + mutate() computes within-sample quantities such as counts-per-million (CPM), summarise() collapses groups to one summary row, and arrange() sorts results:

# Run interactively in R after sourcing scripts/01-tidy-qc.R (uses the 9-row `joined` tibble):
gene_summary <- joined %>%
  select(gene, sample_id, condition, raw_count) %>%
  group_by(sample_id) %>%
  mutate(sample_cpm = (raw_count / sum(raw_count)) * 1e6) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(raw_count >= 150) %>%
  group_by(gene, condition) %>%
  summarise(
    n_samples = n(),
    mean_raw_count = mean(raw_count),
    mean_sample_cpm = round(mean(sample_cpm), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_raw_count), gene)

print(gene_summary)

Expected summary on the 3-gene x 3-sample fixture (notice that within every sample, the three sample_cpm values sum to 1,000,000, unlike total_counts_millions which rescales the library total):

MYC    treated            2           910.0         664215.8
MYC    control            1           890.0         654411.8
BRCA1  control            1           320.0         235294.1
BRCA1  treated            2           292.5         213539.8
TP53   treated            2           167.5         122244.4
TP53   control            1           150.0         110294.1

Diagnose common failures

  • Missing or extra sample columns: the setequal() check stops unless the count-column names and metadata IDs match exactly. Inspect setdiff(count_samples, samples$sample_id) and the reverse comparison. Standardize whitespace or case only when the identifier source confirms that transformation is appropriate.
  • Duplicate metadata IDs: the uniqueness assertion stops before the join. A duplicated key can multiply gene-sample rows; correct or explain the metadata records rather than accepting inflated totals.
  • Missing metadata after join: stopifnot(!anyNA(joined$condition)) catches unmatched or missing condition values. Check keys and missing condition values separately; left_join() preserves count rows while unmatched metadata fields become missing.
  • Counts fail validation: investigate blank values, text, non-finite values, or negative entries in the source file. A missing count is not interchangeable with zero, so do not replace missing values without a documented data-specific reason.
  • Root or input path is wrong: check getwd(), the local .here file and the script location. Rerun the complete script from tidy-qc; here::i_am() should resolve this lab even inside an ancestor Git repository. If you move or rename the script, update that declaration to match.
  • Output write fails: this script creates results/, but permissions or an incorrect project root can still prevent writing. Inspect here() and the exact output path.

A two-step multi-sample Snakemake workflow

Snakemake builds a directed acyclic graph (DAG) backward from requested target files (rule all) to raw inputs using filename wildcards. To see real workflow scheduling rather than a single file copy, the Snakefile below processes two sample fixtures (sampleA and sampleB) in parallel (summarize_sample), declares per-rule software environments (conda:) and Slurm-ready compute budgets (threads and resources), and then aggregates all sample outputs in a fan-in rule (merge_cohort):

SAMPLES = ["sampleA", "sampleB"]

rule all:
    input:
        "results/cohort_line_counts.tsv"

rule summarize_sample:
    input:
        txt="data/{sample}.txt"
    output:
        tsv="results/per_sample/{sample}.lines.tsv"
    log:
        "logs/summarize_{sample}.log"
    conda:
        "envs/coreutils.yaml"
    threads: 1
    resources:
        mem_mb=1000,
        runtime=10
    shell:
        """
        mkdir -p results/per_sample logs
        lines=$(wc -l < {input.txt:q})
        printf '%s\t%s\n' {wildcards.sample:q} "$lines" > {output.tsv:q} 2> {log:q}
        """

rule merge_cohort:
    input:
        expand("results/per_sample/{sample}.lines.tsv", sample=SAMPLES)
    output:
        "results/cohort_line_counts.tsv"
    resources:
        mem_mb=500,
        runtime=5
    shell:
        """
        printf 'sample_id\tline_count\n' > {output:q}
        cat {input:q} >> {output:q}
        """

Save this as Snakefile, create data/sampleA.txt and data/sampleB.txt, and inspect the planned 3-job execution graph first with snakemake -n -p (dry run printing shell commands) before executing locally with snakemake --cores 2 (or snakemake --cores 2 --sdm conda when instantiating per-rule Conda environments in Snakemake 8+). Because merge_cohort lists expand("results/per_sample/{sample}.lines.tsv", sample=SAMPLES) as its input, Snakemake schedules both summarize_sample jobs concurrently when two cores are available and waits for both to finish before writing results/cohort_line_counts.tsv. On an HPC cluster, those same threads and resources blocks map directly to Slurm job requests via snakemake --executor slurm --jobs 20 (see HPC Job Submission).

Before adapting the rule: confirm that every output path is unique per sample, every input exists, and the command really creates the file declared under output. A command that exits successfully while leaving a truncated file can still mislead downstream steps.

Dry runs and failures

Use snakemake -n before a larger run to inspect the jobs Snakemake plans to execute without running them. A missing input should stop rule planning or execution with an informative error. If a result is unexpectedly considered current, inspect the target, input paths, timestamps, and whether the rule fully declares the files it creates. A dry run checks the planned graph; it does not validate the scientific suitability of the commands.

A small Snakemake workflow

Snakemake describes rules with inputs and outputs. The requested target determines which rules are needed; wildcard patterns let one rule describe the same operation for multiple sample names. This synthetic example copies one plain-text fixture to a results directory so you can check the mechanics without installing a bioinformatics tool.

SAMPLES = ["demo"]

rule all:
    input:
        expand("results/{sample}.txt", sample=SAMPLES)

rule copy_fixture:
    input:
        "data/{sample}.txt"
    output:
        "results/{sample}.txt"
    shell:
        "cp {input:q} {output:q}"

The default target is rule all; its expanded input names the desired result, and Snakemake matches that path to copy_fixture. The {sample} wildcard is inferred from the target and substituted into the input path. The :q formatter quotes paths passed to the shell command. Inspect results/demo.txt and compare it with the input. This is a software fixture, not evidence about a sequencing analysis.

Nextflow records task cache entries on each run, but reuses them only when you explicitly pass -resume. Use nextflow run main.nf -resume to request reuse when the task is eligible; keep the associated cache and work directories. Choose by workflow architecture: Snakemake vs Nextflow

Snakemake vs Nextflow technical comparison
DimensionSnakemake (Molder et al., 2021)Nextflow DSL2 (Di Tommaso et al., 2017)
Scheduling modelPull-based backward chaining: starts from requested target paths (rule all) and resolves upstream rules via filename wildcards.Push-based dataflow: channels emit items or tuple val(sample_id), path(reads) objects into downstream processes as soon as upstream tasks finish.
Working directory & stagingRuns in the project working tree writing directly to declared paths; metadata and Conda prefixes live under .snakemake/.Runs every task inside an isolated hash directory (work/ab/cdef123.../) with symlinked inputs; copies selected outputs via publishDir.
Resume semanticsSkips rules whose outputs exist and are newer than inputs (plus code/param provenance checks in Snakemake 8+); re-evaluates automatically.Re-runs from scratch by default unless you pass -resume, which matches cached task hashes in work/.
Software & HPC directivesPer-rule conda: "envs/tool.yaml" or container: "docker://..." plus threads: and resources: mem_mb=..., runtime=...; Slurm via --executor slurm.Per-process conda or container 'quay.io/biocontainers/...' plus cpus, memory, time; Slurm via process.executor = 'slurm' in nextflow.config.

Consider Snakemake when your analysis naturally centers on predictable directory trees, R/Python custom scripts, and file-target wildcards.

Consider Nextflow (or nf-core) when sample sheets drive complex multi-branch channel routing across local workstations, Slurm clusters, and cloud object stores, or when a peer-reviewed nf-core pipeline (Ewels et al., 2020) already matches your assay.

Neither choice guarantees biological validity on its own. Version-control the workflow and configuration, pin container digests or Conda lockfiles, and retain run logs and output checksums.

Running an nf-core pipeline safely

nf-core pipelines are versioned community workflows with their own input schemas and parameters. Do not copy an invocation without checking the pipeline's current documentation. For nf-core/rnaseq, the official usage page documents a samplesheet and requires reference inputs such as a genome FASTA and annotation GTF for the relevant configuration. Always pin an explicit release tag with -r (for example nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq -r 3.14.0 -profile test,singularity --outdir results_test) rather than pulling a mutable branch. The test profile verifies your executor and container setup, not your study design, sample sheet, or reference build.

Exercise: test a two-sample dependency graph

  1. Create data/sampleA.txt (3 lines) and data/sampleB.txt (5 lines), run snakemake -n -p to inspect the 3-job DAG, and then run snakemake --cores 2 (omitting or commenting conda: if testing with system coreutils).
  2. Add "sampleC" to SAMPLES without creating data/sampleC.txt, run snakemake -n, and verify that planning halts with MissingInputException before touching existing outputs.
  3. Create data/sampleC.txt, rerun, and verify that Snakemake runs summarize_sample only for sampleC before updating merge_cohort.

Check your reasoning: incremental re-execution proves dependency tracking, not read quality, strand orientation, or alignment accuracy.

Choose by workflow needs, not labels

Consider Snakemake when a rule-and-file dependency graph maps naturally to the way your team already describes analysis steps, or when Python-based rule definitions suit your group.

Consider Nextflow when the team prefers process/channel dataflow or needs to target execution environments supported by its configuration and infrastructure. Avoid using a mutable “latest” workflow or an unreviewed parameter file for a long-lived analysis. Keep credentials and private data out of the workflow repository and logs.
