How to read the result without over-interpreting it:

  • Finding discrete clusters that correspond to known immune cell types (e.g., T cells, B cells, monocytes) is consistent with expected biology in PBMC samples. In the public PBMC 3k benchmark, canonical marker panels typically separate naive and memory CD4+ T cells (IL7R, CCR7, S100A4), CD8+ T cells (CD8A), NK cells (GNLY, NKG7, CD3D-low), B cells (MS4A1, CD79A), classical CD14+ monocytes (CD14, LYZ), non-classical FCGR3A+ monocytes (FCGR3A, MS4A7), dendritic cells (FCER1A, CST3), and platelets/megakaryocyte fragments (PPBP). Even clear marker enrichment remains expression-derived; orthogonal assays (flow cytometry, CITE-seq surface antibodies) strengthen cell-type claims.
  • Beyond fixed teaching cutoffs (200-2,500 genes and <5% mitochondrial counts), multi-sample production pipelines combine sample-specific median-absolute-deviation (MAD) outlier rules (for example scuttle::isOutlier), explicit heterotypic doublet callers (scDblFinder in R or Scrublet in Python), and ambient cell-free RNA decontamination (SoupX or CellBender) when droplet background is high.
  • Detecting a small cluster with high n_genes and n_counts might indicate doublets but could also be a biologically large or activated cell type (such as proliferating plasmablasts). Do not automatically remove such clusters without checking marker co-expression (for example simultaneous CD3D and MS4A1).
  • A visually separated UMAP is neither necessary nor sufficient evidence of biological validity: batch effects, normalization artifacts, or inappropriate gene selection can create misleading visual separation. Validate the analysis with markers, technical-covariate checks, and relevant biological evidence.

Fixes: Re-examine experimental protocol; increase mito cutoff if cells are known to be mitochondrial-rich (e.g., muscle), but document the rationale. Consider removing cells with extreme percent.mt values and check downstream impact.
  • Symptom: Clusters correlate with n_counts or percent.mt rather than biological markers.
    Likely causes: Technical variation dominating the signal (batch effects, library size differences).
    Fixes: Regress out technical covariates during scaling (for example ScaleData(..., vars.to.regress = c("nCount_RNA", "percent.mt")) in Seurat) or apply multi-sample integration (Harmony, Seurat v5 IntegrateLayers, or scVI) when combining distinct batches.
  • Symptom: Too many small clusters or over-clustering.
    Likely causes: High clustering resolution or too many PCs with noise.
    Fixes: Lower clustering resolution (e.g., from 1.0 to 0.4), reduce number of PCs, or merge clusters based on marker gene expression.
  • Symptom: No clear elbow in PCA variance plot.
    Likely causes: Gradual decay of variance due to continuous biological gradients or high noise.
    Fixes: Inspect top PC gene loadings (VizDimLoadings / DimHeatmap) and evaluate whether cluster identities and biological markers remain stable across a sensible PC range (for example 15, 25, and 35 PCs). Note that Seurat's older JackStraw permutation test is computationally slow, legacy, and incompatible with SCTransform workflows.

A better-mixed UMAP is not enough to justify integration. This worked example compares an unintegrated PCA representation with Harmony on exactly the same public PBMC cells, then asks two separate questions: did batch diversity change, and what happened to the purity of the supplied cell-type labels?

Format: Hands-on lab. The public-data PCA → Harmony workflow and LISI calculations were executed for this lesson. Scripts, selected cell IDs, settings, environment records and observed results are downloadable. RPCA and CCA are discussed as unexecuted extensions; this page does not report their performance.

  • Design and inputs
  • Run the example
  • Observed comparison
  • Interpret the trade-off
  • RPCA and CCA extensions

1. Start with a comparison the data can support

We use the public pbmcsca.SeuratData 3.0.0 dataset from SeuratData, based on Ding et al.'s systematic comparison of sequencing methods. The two query groups are 10x Chromium (v2) A and 10x Chromium (v3): genuine assay groups, not an artificial split of one count matrix. A third group is reserved for the separate annotation lesson and does not enter this integration comparison.

The recorded public-data selection
Source Method Role Source cells Eligible cells Selected
10x Chromium (v2) A Query 3222 2992 590
10x Chromium (v2) B Reference 3222 3011 537
10x Chromium (v3) Query 3222 2993 559

The workflow retains cells with more than 200 detected genes and usable supplied CellType annotations, then takes at most 80 cells per assay-group × source-label stratum with a fixed seed and stable ordering. Smaller strata are retained. The query has 1,149 cells across 9 supplied source-label categories; exact selections and exclusions are recorded. This capped sample is deliberately compact and label-stratified, so neither cell-type frequencies nor score distributions represent the full study or natural blood composition.

Why integration is a question, not an obligation. Shared populations make a comparison possible, but an assay label can still be confounded with donor, processing, depth or genuine state. If comparable populations already mix, correction may add little. A type seen in only one batch has no demonstrated counterpart to align. Keep the baseline and check the batch-by-label composition before interpreting any score.

2. Run one recorded preprocessing path

Download the worked-example bundle, follow its setup and reproduction notes, and inspect the full executable script. The input is fetched from its public provider and checked against a recorded SHA-256; no private data or pre-existing local RDS object is required.

cd pbmc-methods-worked-example

dims.use = 1:20, theta = 2, lambda = 1, max_iter = 10, ncores = 1 )

In RunHarmony, theta = 2 sets the soft-cluster diversity penalty (higher theta forces stronger cross-batch mixing within soft centroids, increasing overcorrection risk when cell types are unshared across batches) and lambda = 1 sets the ridge-regression penalty that stabilizes the linear batch-offset step across iterations. Integration does not manufacture biological replicates: cells are not independent donor replicates, and corrected coordinates are not corrected gene counts for differential expression. Keep the original RNA assay and use a suitable sample-aware inferential design for downstream expression comparisons.

The calculation uses lisi::compute_lisi() on the 20-dimensional coordinates, not UMAP, with perplexity 30 for both branches. Coordinate rows, metadata rows and cell IDs must match exactly. Missing labels, duplicate IDs, too few cells or a different cell set cause the workflow to stop.

Two labels, two different questions
Diagnostic What it measures here What it does not establish
Batch iLISI Effective local number of assay-group labels. With two groups, 1 indicates local dominance by one group; values approaching 2 indicate greater diversity. A universal target of 2, removal of a causal technical effect, or permission to mix distinct states.
Source-label cLISI Effective local number of supplied cell-type labels. Values near 1 mean greater source-label purity. Independent biological validation, correct labels, or preservation of every rare state and continuous trajectory.

These are raw local-diversity diagnostics, not normalized benchmark scores. Neighborhood scale, category proportions, embedding geometry and label quality affect their values. The source labels are pre-existing expression-derived annotations (not clusters newly defined from Harmony), but they still are not independent ground truth. No silhouette or held-out biological validation is reported.

4. Inspect the observed comparison

Saved run: The same 1,149 query cells were scored in 20-dimensional PCA and Harmony representations; the reference cells were not included in integration.

Observed raw LISI scores: median [25th–75th percentile]
Representation Cells Batch iLISI Source-label cLISI
PCA 1,149 1.066 [1.011–1.257] 1.016 [1.001–1.140]
Harmony 1,149 1.918 [1.789–1.979] 1.008 [1.000–1.091]

Median batch diversity increases from 1.066 to 1.918, while the pooled source-label purity diagnostic remains close to 1. This supports a limited mixing interpretation for the annotated sample, not a claim that all biological structure was preserved. The median paired iLISI change is 0.766; that is not the same quantity as subtracting the two pooled medians.

Do not let a pooled median hide a population

The bundle includes paired per-cell scores and summaries by source label. Compare each category with its own baseline, and consult the actual batch counts: a rare group or a label missing from one batch cannot be interpreted like a balanced shared population.

5. Make a bounded decision

The pooled comparison is consistent with improved assay-group mixing: median batch iLISI rises from 1.066 to 1.918, while median source-label cLISI stays close to 1 (1.016 → 1.008). But the 26 plasmacytoid dendritic cells are all from v2 A; their median cLISI increases from 1.360 to 1.529. Their neighborhoods can gain batch diversity by containing other annotated types, not by finding a demonstrated same-type v3 counterpart. Their small size relative to perplexity 30 also makes neighborhood-scale effects important. This does not prove overcorrection, but it is a concrete reason to investigate that population rather than accepting the pooled median as a universal success signal. These diagnostics are not independent biological validation.

  • Batch diversity rises while source-label purity stays similar: evidence consistent with improved mixing of those annotated categories. It is not proof of preserved function or rare-state structure.
  • Batch and source-label diversity both rise: inspect possible overcorrection, annotation errors or genuine transitional states before accepting the representation.
  • Batch diversity barely changes: the baseline may already mix, or correction may not address the relevant effect. Increasing correction strength is not automatically appropriate.
  • A population moves unexpectedly: check cell identity, source-label reliability, original RNA marker expression, depth and batch composition before blaming or endorsing the algorithm.

The annotation lesson's RNA marker plot supplies an expression-derived cross-check on these same query cells. Harmony leaving RNA unchanged does not prove that its embedding preserves biology; marker evidence, rare-population inspection and independent measurements remain necessary for stronger claims.

Practice: retain, investigate or reject?

Choose one source-label category. Record its cell counts in both groups, its baseline and Harmony iLISI/cLISI summaries, and one RNA marker observation. Make a retain/investigate/reject decision for that limited purpose and state what additional evidence would change your mind. Do not infer population-level significance from cell-level scores.

6. Choosing across integration method families

Unexecuted extensions. RPCA, CCA, scVI, and scANVI were not run for this saved example. No benchmark rankings or runtimes are claimed from this subset; consult large multi-task benchmarks such as Luecken et al. (2022, scIB) for cross-atlas evidence.

Method classes, corrected outputs, and typical failure modes
Method What it corrects Scaling Primary failure mode to audit
Harmony (RunHarmony) Low-dimensional linear embedding (PC coordinates only; counts unchanged). Fast; scales to >105-106 cells on CPU. High theta can pull batch-unique or disease-restricted states into unrelated shared clusters.
Seurat v5 RPCA (IntegrateLayers(..., RPCAIntegration)) Reciprocal-PCA anchors producing an integrated low-dim reduction (or optional reconstructed layer). Fast and memory-efficient for large cohorts and reference mapping. More conservative than CCA; can under-align strong cross-chemistry or cross-species shifts.
Seurat v5 CCA (CCAIntegration) Canonical correlation anchors maximizing shared covariance across batches. Quadratic memory/time growth across many large batches. Prone to overcorrection when biological composition differs sharply (for example tumor vs healthy tissue).
scVI / scANVI (scvi-tools) Deep variational autoencoder directly modeling raw UMI counts with batch covariates (plus partial labels in scANVI). Scales to millions of cells (GPU-accelerated). Sensitive to HVG count, latent dimensionality, and epoch tuning; scANVI generally outperforms unsupervised methods on bio-conservation in scIB when reliable seed labels exist.

Seurat's RPCA and CCA workflows find anchors between datasets rather than applying the same iterative soft-clustering correction as Harmony. Use the current Seurat v5 IntegrateLayers vignette and RPCA guide for the API matching your object version.

To extend this experiment fairly, preserve the same selected cells, source labels and dimensions policy; record any method-specific preprocessing; align every branch by cell ID; rerun the same diagnostic calculations (or try a small sensitivity sweep across theta = 1, 2, 4); and inspect original RNA markers and rare populations. Different integration assays and corrected coordinates are not interchangeable with raw counts.

5. Make a bounded decision

The pooled comparison is consistent with improved assay-group mixing: median batch iLISI rises from 1.066 to 1.918, while median source-label cLISI stays close to 1 (1.016 → 1.008). But the 26 plasmacytoid dendritic cells are all from v2 A; their median cLISI increases from 1.360 to 1.529. Their neighborhoods can gain batch diversity by containing other annotated types, not by finding a demonstrated same-type v3 counterpart. Their small size relative to perplexity 30 also makes neighborhood-scale effects important. This does not prove overcorrection, but it is a concrete reason to investigate that population rather than accepting the pooled median as a universal success signal. These diagnostics are not independent biological validation.

  • Batch diversity rises while source-label purity stays similar: evidence consistent with improved mixing of those annotated categories. It is not proof of preserved function or rare-state structure.
  • Batch and source-label diversity both rise: inspect possible overcorrection, annotation errors or genuine transitional states before accepting the representation.
  • Batch diversity barely changes: the baseline may already mix, or correction may not address the relevant effect. Increasing correction strength is not automatically appropriate.
  • A population moves unexpectedly: check cell identity, source-label reliability, original RNA marker expression, depth and batch composition before blaming or endorsing the algorithm.

The annotation lesson's RNA marker plot supplies an expression-derived cross-check on these same query cells. Harmony leaving RNA unchanged does not prove that its embedding preserves biology; marker evidence, rare-population inspection and independent measurements remain necessary for stronger claims.

Practice: retain, investigate or reject?

Choose one source-label category. Record its cell counts in both groups, its baseline and Harmony iLISI/cLISI summaries, and one RNA marker observation. Make a retain/investigate/reject decision for that limited purpose and state what additional evidence would change your mind. Do not infer population-level significance from cell-level scores.

6. Where RPCA and CCA fit

Unexecuted extensions. RPCA and CCA were not run for this saved example. No results, runtimes or method-ranking claims are supplied for them.

Seurat's RPCA and CCA workflows find anchors between datasets rather than applying the same embedding-correction algorithm as Harmony. RPCA is described in Seurat's documentation as a more conservative alignment option; that general description does not predict which representation is appropriate for this dataset. Use the current integration vignette and RPCA guide for the API matching your object version.

To extend this experiment fairly, preserve the same selected cells, source labels and dimensions policy; record any method-specific preprocessing; align every branch by cell ID; rerun the same diagnostic calculations; and inspect original RNA markers and rare populations. Add RPCA/CCA rows only after those branches actually run. Different integration assays and corrected coordinates are not interchangeable with raw counts.

Format: Conceptual guide. For learners who already have a quality-controlled, clustered single-cell object, this guide compares trajectory assumptions and walks through method-specific inspection examples. Bring your own processed data and justify its root, representation, and cluster labels; no dataset is supplied.

Understanding Trajectory Inference and When Not to Use It

Single-cell RNA-seq measures cells at collection, not their histories. Trajectory inference orders cells along a transcriptional manifold ("pseudotime") only when the sampled cohort actually captures intermediate states of a continuous biological transition. Similarity-based ordering alone does not prove that one cell differentiates into another, nor does it measure elapsed clock time.

First check biological continuity and expected topology (Saelens et al., 2019): do not run trajectory inference on steady-state peripheral blood (PBMC 3k), where mature B cells, NK cells, monocytes, and resting T cells represent terminally differentiated lineages whose bone-marrow and thymic progenitors are absent from peripheral blood. Appropriate trajectory systems capture intermediate transition states directly, such as bone-marrow hematopoiesis (for example myeloid vs erythroid branching in Paul et al., 2015), intestinal crypt-to-villus epithelial differentiation, or intratumoural CD8+ T-cell differentiation from TCF7+ SLAMF6+ progenitor-exhausted cells toward HAVCR2+ CXCL13+ terminally exhausted states. Match the method family to the expected topology: tree/lineage principal curves (Slingshot), disconnected-capable partition graphs (PAGA + DPT), or principal graphs (Monocle3), and use RNA splicing kinetics (scVelo, Bergen et al., 2020) or metabolic/lineage barcoding with care when independent directional evidence is needed, bearing in mind multi-rate transcription caveats (Bergen et al., 2021).

PAGA summarizes connectivity among chosen partitions; DPT assigns a diffusion-based ordering relative to a named root cell. Slingshot fits lineages from clusters in a reduced-dimensional space, while Monocle3 learns a principal graph. Because their underlying spaces and graph assumptions differ, their outputs are not interchangeable. Fit lineages in a reviewed high-dimensional representation such as PCA or diffusion space whenever the method allows it, reserving 2D UMAP strictly for display.

R (primary): Slingshot lineage inference

Slingshot uses cluster labels and coordinates in a reduced-dimensional space to build a cluster-based minimum spanning tree and fit simultaneous principal curves along each lineage (Street et al., 2018). This example fits curves in reviewed PCA coordinates and then colors a separate UMAP display by pseudotime without projecting PCA curves onto UMAP geometry. Note that Seurat::as.SingleCellExperiment() is provided directly by Seurat (no SeuratWrappers install needed; in Seurat v5, run JoinLayers() first if per-sample layers are split). Supply an object containing a genuine developmental or activation continuum (lineage_obj), never steady-state PBMC. 

library(Seurat)
library(slingshot)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
library(RColorBrewer)

# Supply a continuous-process Seurat object (e.g. bone-marrow progenitors), NOT steady-state PBMC.
if (length(Layers(lineage_obj, search = 'data')) > 1L) lineage_obj <- JoinLayers(lineage_obj)
sce <- as.SingleCellExperiment(lineage_obj)

# Confirm conversion preserved the reviewed inference space, display space, and labels.
if (!all(c('PCA', 'UMAP') %in% reducedDimNames(sce))) stop('Expected both PCA and UMAP reductions.')

Trajectory inference (TI) algorithms attempt to order cells along a learned trajectory based on their transcriptional similarities, creating a "pseudotime" axis. This allows us to track gene expression changes as cells differentiate.

For inference, use a reviewed high-dimensional representation such as PCA or the expression space appropriate to the analysis. UMAP is a display, not a substitute for that inference space.

R (primary): Slingshot lineage inference

This example fits in reviewed PCA coordinates. It then colors a separate UMAP display by the returned pseudotime without drawing PCA-fit curves in UMAP geometry. Conversion from Seurat uses SeuratWrappers; check that the intended clustering and both named representations were carried into the SingleCellExperiment object before inference.

library(slingshot)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
library(RColorBrewer)

# Convert Seurat object to SingleCellExperiment (SCE)

# Confirm conversion preserved the reviewed inference space, display space, and labels.
if (!all(c('PCA', 'UMAP') %in% reducedDimNames(sce))) stop('Expected both PCA and UMAP reductions.')

⚠️ Pitfalls to Avoid

The explicitly selected start cluster sets orientation; it does not validate that a lineage exists. Replace the placeholder only after stating why that cluster is a plausible start, confirm it is present, and compare defensible alternatives. PCA distances and UMAP distances are not interchangeable, so inspect fitted curves in their fitted PCA representation if curve geometry is needed.

Exploring expression along inferred lineages

The tradeSeq package fits negative-binomial generalized additive models to count data using pseudotime and lineage weights. Its tests identify expression patterns associated with the fitted ordering; they do not establish causal driver genes.

The inputs must be aligned by cell: rows of the count matrix are genes and columns are cells; pseudotime and cell-weight matrices have cells by lineages. Select the knot count with the package guidance, inspect per-gene convergence, and account for multiple testing when interpreting results. `associationTest` tests association with pseudotime; `startVsEndTest` compares fitted expression at lineage endpoints.

R (primary): Monocle3 principal graph and root

Monocle3 uses its own cell_data_set representation and learns a principal graph directly on the low-dimensional UMAP embedding by default (learn_graph(cds) uses reduction_method = "UMAP"; Cao et al., 2019). Because 2D UMAP layouts can compress or tear global manifold distances, inspect whether apparent branches or bridges persist across reasonable UMAP neighbor settings and independent PAGA/PCA checks before interpreting them biologically. Conversion from Seurat requires SeuratWrappers::as.cell_data_set() (installed from GitHub), and root selection must be supplied explicitly from known early-state cells. 

library(monocle3)
library(SeuratWrappers)

# Convert a continuous-process Seurat object to CellDataSet (CDS)
cds <- as.cell_data_set(lineage_obj)

# 1. Calculate size factors and partition/cluster cells within Monocle3
cds <- estimate_size_factors(cds)
cds <- cluster_cells(cds, reduction_method = "UMAP")

# 2. Learn the principal graph (note: Monocle3 fits this graph in UMAP space)
cds <- learn_graph(cds, use_partition = TRUE)

# 3. Inspect the learned graph and select root_pr_nodes from the graph
# based on known early-state cells; this is not an automatic biological decision.

Monocle3 uses its own cell_data_set representation and workflow. A Seurat conversion is not guaranteed to preserve the intended clusters or embeddings; inspect the converted object and follow the package-specific trajectory guidance. Root selection is explicit and can be given as root principal-graph nodes or root cells supported by the data.

library(SeuratWrappers)

# 1. Calculate size factors and cluster cells within Monocle
cds <- estimate_size_factors(cds)
cds <- cluster_cells(cds)

Understanding the Output

Monocle3 stores expression data and cell/gene metadata in a cell_data_set object. Disconnected partitions receive separate graphs when use_partition = TRUE (giving unrelated lineages infinite pseudotime relative to a single root rather than forcing a spurious bridge). Inspect graph nodes with plot_cells(cds, label_principal_points = TRUE) before ordering cells.

⚠️ Pitfalls to Avoid

Unlike Slingshot (which fits in PCA) and DPT (which operates on the high-dimensional PCA neighbor diffusion operator), Monocle3's learn_graph() fits its tree/graph directly in UMAP coordinates. Treat UMAP-derived branch geometry with extra caution, check sensitivity to preprocess_cds() / reduce_dimension() settings, and verify that as.cell_data_set() carried over the intended counts and UMAP coordinates.

Optional Python method (distinct): Scanpy PAGA and DPT

This is not a Python translation of Slingshot or Monocle3. PAGA summarizes partition connectivity and DPT orders cells relative to a chosen root on a neighbor graph; their assumptions and outputs differ from the R lineage and principal-graph methods above. Use the existing Python template only if this graph-based question suits your analysis, and do not treat similarly shaped pseudotime plots as equivalent evidence.

Partition-based Graph Abstraction (PAGA) is integrated directly into the Scanpy system. It generates a coarse-grained map of cellular connectivity and provides a solid scaffold for embedding and pseudotime calculation.

Understanding the Output

PAGA edge weights summarize connectivity between the chosen partitions in the explicitly named neighbor graph. The DPT graph is built from reviewed PCA coordinates here. UMAP is used only to display cells colored by DPT; its two-dimensional distances and apparent paths are not the fitted trajectory. The code reuses the graph only when Scanpy's stored key, representation, PC count, neighbor count, method, metric, and random state all match. Otherwise it stops until you explicitly approve rebuilding, and it records the graph action and settings.

⚠️ Pitfalls to Avoid

The graph depends on both the neighbor graph and the partition labels. Compare reasonable clustering choices and inspect whether proposed edges have support in the underlying cells. The example validates two named root cells against a declared early-state annotation, records each rationale, and compares both rootings. It masks cells outside each root's connected component as unassigned for this interpretation; it does not turn a disconnected population into a continuous path.

Mini contract exercise: a known invented graph

This teaching-only graph has edges A0 to A1, A1 to M, M to L, and M to R, plus a disconnected component X to Y. A0 and A1 are both annotated as the supported early state; M is intermediate, and L/R are two terminal sampled groups. No biological data are represented.

Predict before reading on: If A0 is the named root, which cells are reachable and what broad ordering would you expect? If A1 is a second defensible root from the same early state, what changes? Which cells must not receive a root-relative interpretation?

Worked answer and explanation

For ordinary shortest-path distance on this invented unweighted graph, root A0 gives A0:0, A1:1, M:2, and L/R:3. Root A1 gives A1:0, A0 and M:1, and L/R:2. These integer distances are only a hand-check of graph reachability and root sensitivity, not the numeric output promised by DPT, which uses diffusion geometry. X and Y remain disconnected from either root and are unassigned for that root-relative interpretation. A changed ordering after changing roots is expected sensitivity, not evidence of a changed biological clock. Even a stable ordering is a model of sampled expression structure, not observed time, cell ancestry, or future fate.

Compare methods and review the result

For each saved figure, record the root (including how it was chosen), embedding and coordinate fields, clustering/partition field, and the observed lineage or branch labels. Label the root on the plot and distinguish fitted paths from cluster-level connectivity. Add a caption stating that pseudotime is relative ordering, identify disconnected or unassigned cells, and note which plausible root, cell-selection, batch, clustering, or representation alternatives were checked. A plot that omits these details is not a complete review record.

Use PAGA to inspect cluster connectivity, then use DPT when a root-relative ordering on the cell graph addresses your question. Use Slingshot when cluster labels and a reduced-dimensional representation support the lineage model you want to test. Monocle3 learns a principal graph with its own workflow. Record the input cells, representation, cluster labels, root choice, and software versions so the analysis can be reviewed.

Before interpreting a branch

  • Does the root label/node correspond to the proposed early state, and are there cells from that state?
  • Do changes in cell selection, clustering, batch handling, or representation alter the path?
  • Are known markers or independent time-course/lineage evidence consistent with the ordering?
  • Are disconnected populations or missing intermediate states being mistaken for a continuous process?

Do not automatically regress out cell-cycle or stress signals: first determine whether they are nuisance variation or part of the biological process under study.

Format: Conceptual guide. For analysts with prepared bulk counts and an annotated single-cell reference, this guide walks through input review, a MuSiC fit scaffold, and interpretation checks. No data are supplied; readers must prepare both objects and their metadata.

Scope and inputs

MuSiC is a reference-based method designed to use cross-subject single-cell data. You need bulk gene-expression measurements and a single-cell reference with gene counts, cell-type labels, and donor/sample IDs. The code below is an analysis scaffold: replace the named objects and metadata fields with your data, and verify package versions and preprocessing before running it.

What the estimate means and how MuSiC weights genes

A bulk profile is modeled as a non-negative linear combination of reference cell-type profiles. MuSiC (Wang et al., 2019) improves on ordinary unweighted non-negative least squares (NNLS) through three design choices that every analyst should check against their cohort:

  • Cross-subject variance weighting: instead of requiring a fixed pre-selected marker gene list, MuSiC estimates gene-specific cross-donor variance from a multi-subject single-cell reference. Genes with low cross-subject variance (stable lineage markers across donors) receive high weight, whereas genes that fluctuate sharply across donors (dissociation-induced immediate-early genes, interferon bursts, or ambient RNA contaminants) are downweighted automatically.
  • Cell-size scaling (cell_size): metabolically active macrophages, plasma cells, and malignant epithelial cells contain substantially more total mRNA per cell than resting naive lymphocytes. MuSiC accounts for library-size differences per cell type so that estimated proportions reflect cell fractions rather than raw mRNA mass; you can inspect or supply custom cell sizes via the cell_size argument in music_prop().
  • Tree-guided recursive deconvolution: when closely related subpopulations (for example naive CD4+, memory CD4+, regulatory T, and exhausted CD8+ T cells) share highly collinear expression profiles, flat single-step NNLS suffers variance inflation and unstable trade-offs between sibling clusters. MuSiC's tree-guided mode (music_prop.cluster()) groups collinear clusters into broad parent lineages first, estimates parent proportions using lineage-discriminating genes, and then resolves child subtypes within each lineage.

Estimated fractions remain strictly conditional on the cell types represented in the reference. If a major population is absent, or if reference and bulk samples differ substantially in tissue, disease state, or RNA extraction chemistry (for example poly(A) single-cell capture vs ribo-depleted FFPE bulk RNA-seq), NNLS redistributes the unmodeled signal across the closest available reference profiles while still normalizing the reported fractions to sum to 1.0. Estimating proportions also does not establish that a cell population caused a clinical phenotype; outcome associations require an independent sample-level statistical model.

Check the reference before fitting

  1. Confirm cell-type annotations and donor identifiers are present for every reference cell. MuSiC uses the cell-type field as clusters and donor/sample field as samples.

Format: Conceptual guide. For analysts with prepared bulk counts and an annotated single-cell reference, this guide walks through input review, a MuSiC fit scaffold, and interpretation checks. No data are supplied; readers must prepare both objects and their metadata.

Scope and inputs

MuSiC is a reference-based method designed to use cross-subject single-cell data. You need bulk gene-expression measurements and a single-cell reference with gene counts, cell-type labels, and donor/sample IDs. The code below is an analysis scaffold: replace the named objects and metadata fields with your data, and verify package versions and preprocessing before running it.

What the estimate means

A bulk profile is modeled as a mixture of reference cell-type profiles. The estimated fractions depend on the cell types and expression states represented in that reference. If a relevant population is absent, or if reference and bulk samples differ substantially in condition, tissue, platform, or processing, the model may assign its signal to the closest represented populations. A precise decimal does not remove this ambiguity.

MuSiC's weighting uses cross-subject variation in the single-cell reference. The method estimates proportions; it does not establish that a cell population caused a clinical outcome. Associations with outcomes require a separate, appropriately designed analysis.

Check the reference before fitting

  1. Confirm cell-type annotations and donor identifiers are present for every reference cell. MuSiC uses the cell-type field as clusters and donor/sample field as samples.

The identifier columns cell_type and donor_id are examples, not required names; change them to columns actually present in colData(sc_reference). MuSiC uses genes shared between the bulk matrix and reference when markers are left at their default. The output list also contains an all-gene NNLS estimate, gene weights, fit summaries, and variance estimates in the documented implementation. Check the installed version's documentation if an output name differs.

Inspect, plot, and interpret

First inspect dimensions, sample names, cell-type columns, missing values, and whether estimates are finite. MuSiC documents estimates normalized across the included cell types. That sum is conditional on the cell types included in the fit; it does not prove that the reference contains every cell population in the tissue.

# Basic output checks; compare cross-subject weighted MuSiC vs unweighted all-gene NNLS.
stopifnot(nrow(prop_estimates) == ncol(bulk_use))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(as.matrix(prop_estimates))))
range(as.matrix(prop_estimates), na.rm = TRUE)
rowSums(as.matrix(prop_estimates))

nnls_estimates <- music_results$Est.prop.allgene
max_method_diff <- apply(abs(as.matrix(prop_estimates) - as.matrix(nnls_estimates)), 2, max)
print(round(max_method_diff, 3))

# Reshape and visualize estimated cell-type proportions across samples (template).
library(ggplot2)
plot_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(as.matrix(prop_estimates)))
names(plot_df) <- c("bulk_sample", "cell_type", "proportion")
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = bulk_sample, y = proportion, fill = cell_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "MuSiC estimated cell-type fractions (conditional on reference)",
    x = "Bulk RNA-seq sample",
    y = "Estimated proportion"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

Comparing music_results$Est.prop.weighted against music_results$Est.prop.allgene is an immediate diagnostic: large discrepancies on a specific cell type warn either that unweighted NNLS is being pulled by high-variance donor-specific genes or that two reference clusters are nearly collinear. Do not treat a stacked bar chart as biological validation; validate against flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, or held-out pseudo-bulk mixtures with known ground-truth fractions.

Worked R validation check: pseudo-bulk mixtures, variance weighting, and omitted tumour populations

Before running MuSiC on patient bulk cohorts, construct artificial pseudo-bulk mixtures from held-out reference donors so you know the exact true fractions. The self-contained base-R script below (executed locally on R 4.6.1; no external packages required) demonstrates two essential deconvolution diagnostics on an invented 3-donor reference: first, how inverse cross-donor variance weighting stabilizes NNLS against a high-variance stress gene (STRESS_VAR); second, how deconvolving a 45%-tumour bulk mixture against an immune-only reference still returns immune proportions summing to 1.000:

set.seed(20261118)
genes <- c("CD3D", "TRBC1", "LYZ", "S100A8", "COL1A1", "STRESS_VAR")

donor_profiles <- list(
  donor_1 = cbind(T_cell = c(42, 38, 1, 0, 0, 15),
                  Monocyte = c(1, 0, 95, 88, 1, 20),
                  Fibroblast = c(0, 0, 2, 1, 160, 10)),
  donor_2 = cbind(T_cell = c(45, 36, 1, 1, 0, 240),
                  Monocyte = c(0, 1, 90, 92, 2, 15),
                  Fibroblast = c(1, 0, 1, 1, 150, 12)),
  donor_3 = cbind(T_cell = c(40, 41, 0, 1, 1, 30),
                  Monocyte = c(1, 0, 98, 85, 1, 210),
                  Fibroblast = c(0, 1, 1, 0, 170, 14))
)
for (d in names(donor_profiles)) rownames(donor_profiles[[d]]) <- genes

arr <- simplify2array(donor_profiles)
X_ref <- apply(arr, c(1, 2), mean)
gene_var <- apply(arr, 1, function(m) mean(apply(m, 1, var)))
w_inv_var <- 1 / (gene_var + 1)

X_heldout <- cbind(
  T_cell     = c(43, 39, 1, 0, 0, 25),
  Monocyte   = c(1, 0, 93, 89, 1, 18),
  Fibroblast = c(0, 0, 1, 1, 158, 280)
)
rownames(X_heldout) <- genes

true_props <- rbind(
  mix_immune_rich = c(T_cell = 0.60, Monocyte = 0.30, Fibroblast = 0.10),
  mix_stroma_rich = c(T_cell = 0.25, Monocyte = 0.25, Fibroblast = 0.50)
)
bulk_syn <- X_heldout %*% t(true_props) * 1000

fit_nnls <- function(X, y, weights = rep(1, nrow(X))) {
  Xw <- X * sqrt(weights)
  yw <- y * sqrt(weights)
  opt <- optim(rep(1 / ncol(X), ncol(X)),
               function(b) sum((yw - as.vector(Xw %*% b))^2),
               method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = rep(0, ncol(X)))
  setNames(opt$par / sum(opt$par), colnames(X))
}

est_unweighted <- t(apply(bulk_syn, 2, function(y) fit_nnls(X_ref, y)))
est_weighted   <- t(apply(bulk_syn, 2, function(y) fit_nnls(X_ref, y, w_inv_var)))
cat(sprintf("MAE unweighted=%.4f | MAE weighted=%.4f\n",
            mean(abs(est_unweighted - true_props)),
            mean(abs(est_weighted - true_props))))
print(round(est_weighted, 3))

# Fit an immune-only reference to a bulk mixture containing 45% unmodeled tumour RNA:
tumour_profile <- c(CD3D = 0, TRBC1 = 0, LYZ = 4, S100A8 = 6, COL1A1 = 22, STRESS_VAR = 190)
bulk_tumour <- (0.35 * X_heldout[, "T_cell"] + 0.20 * X_heldout[, "Monocyte"] + 0.45 * tumour_profile) * 1000
est_omitted <- fit_nnls(X_ref[, c("T_cell", "Monocyte")], bulk_tumour, w_inv_var)
print(round(est_omitted, 3))

Verified output from local execution (Rscript --vanilla, R 4.6.1):

MAE unweighted=0.1227 | MAE weighted=0.0036
                T_cell Monocyte Fibroblast
mix_immune_rich  0.607    0.297      0.096
mix_stroma_rich  0.253    0.251      0.496
  T_cell Monocyte
   0.614    0.386

Notice both diagnostic lessons: when STRESS_VAR spikes in held-out fibroblasts (mix_stroma_rich, true T_cell = 0.250, Fibroblast = 0.500), unweighted NNLS misassigns the stress signal (T_cell = 0.526, Fibroblast = 0.275, MAE = 0.1227), whereas inverse cross-donor variance weighting recovers 0.253, 0.251, 0.496 (MAE = 0.0036). Equally important, when 45% of the bulk RNA comes from an unrepresented malignant population, the two-population immune fit reports T_cell = 0.614, Monocyte = 0.386 (summing cleanly to 1.000 despite missing nearly half the tissue).

Solid-tumour bulk RNA-seq: malignant heterogeneity, purity, and BayesPrism

Deconvolving bulk solid-tumour cohorts (such as TCGA or clinical biopsy trials) poses a specific challenge: non-malignant immune and stromal lineages share conserved transcriptional programs across patients, whereas malignant epithelial or glial cells harbour patient-specific aneuploidy and oncogenic programs that rarely match a single reference donor. When deconvolving tumour bulk RNA-seq:

  • Never use a healthy PBMC or normal-organ reference without accounting for the malignant compartment; otherwise tumour transcripts inflate epithelial, myeloid, or cycling immune estimates.
  • Compare tumour cell-fraction estimates against independent DNA-based tumour purity (ABSOLUTE, ASCAT, sequenza, or pathology slide review) when matched WES/WGS or H&E slides exist.
  • Consider Bayesian tumour-specialized frameworks such as BayesPrism (Chu et al., 2022), which models conserved non-malignant states jointly while updating a patient-specific malignant expression prior, or CIBERSORTx (Newman et al., 2019) when cross-platform batch correction (S-mode / B-mode) is required.

Hypothetical decision check

Imagine a hypothetical fit that reports proportions summing to one across the cell types included in the reference, while a population of interest is not represented there. Does the sum show that the reported fractions are validated tissue proportions?

Reasoned feedback

No. The estimates are conditional on the included reference types, and normalization to one does not show that the reference is exhaustive or that the fit is accurate. An omitted population can make the reported mixture ambiguous. Review reference coverage and fit diagnostics, test stability under defensible reference choices, and compare with an independent measurement from the same samples when available.

When estimates look implausible

Check gene-ID overlap and order, input scale (linear/raw counts vs log-transformed values; see Avila Cobos et al., 2020), missing or mislabelled metadata, reference coverage, and whether multiple reference profiles are too similar to distinguish. Examine MuSiC's fit and variance outputs alongside the proportions. Do not clip, renormalize, or discard unexpected estimates without understanding what produced them.

Analysis record to keep

For each run, record the reference tissue and condition, cell-type and donor fields, preprocessing and expression scale, number of shared genes, included cell types, MuSiC version, output dimensions, weighted-vs-NNLS stability differences, and any pseudo-bulk or orthogonal purity validation.

  • Avila Cobos, F., Alquicira-Hernandez, J., Powell, J. E., Mestdagh, P., & De Preter, K. (2020). Benchmarking of cell type deconvolution pipelines for transcriptomics data. Nature Communications, 11, 5650. doi:10.1038/s41467-020-19015-1
  • Chu, T., Wang, Z., Pe'er, D., & Danko, C. G. (2022). Cell type and gene expression deconvolution with BayesPrism enables Bayesian integrative analysis across bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing in oncology. Nature Cancer, 3, 505-517. doi:10.1038/s43018-022-00356-3

Calculate total_counts before normalization and log transformation, as above. It then records raw counts per spot; recomputing it from log-transformed expression would no longer measure library size. The marker panel uses the processed expression matrix, so its values are on a different scale from the raw-count QC panel.

Squidpy's spatial_scatter is the current image-overlay plotting API. Older Scanpy examples use sc.pl.spatial, but current Scanpy documentation marks it deprecated in favor of Squidpy's plot. A quick success check is: nonzero observations and features; nonempty, finite library-size values; a tissue image visible beneath spatially aligned spots; and a readable color scale for QC and the selected marker. Library size is a QC view, not a universal pass/fail threshold: in mouse brain (V1_Adult_Mouse_Brain), myelinated white-matter fiber tracts (high Mbp) naturally contain far fewer cell somata and 3- to 5-fold lower nCount_Spatial / total_counts than densely packed hippocampal pyramidal layers (high Snap25), just as collagen-rich desmoplastic stroma or necrotic tumour cores yield lower counts than hypercellular carcinoma nests. Applying a flat global UMI floor deletes real anatomical compartments before downstream analysis even starts. If the image is absent or spots are displaced, verify the input's spatial/ files, library key, and image/coordinate scale; if the marker is missing, choose an observed feature and the intended assay/layer.

3. Cluster expression profiles, then inspect their locations

Expression-neighbor clustering groups observations by transcriptional similarity. It does not by itself define spatial domains. Build the expression graph, cluster, and then display cluster labels in tissue coordinates. Note that Seurat's SCTransform + Louvain/SLM clustering and Scanpy's total-count log-normalization + Leiden clustering weight variance differently across high-abundance markers, so exact cluster numbers and minor cortical sub-layer splits will not match one-to-one even when major anatomical compartments (cortex layers, hippocampus, thalamus, white matter, hypothalamus) align closely.

spatial_data <- RunPCA(spatial_data, assay = "SCT", verbose = FALSE)
spatial_data <- FindNeighbors(spatial_data, reduction = "pca", dims = 1:30)

The paired R and Python templates below extend the objects created above (not executed in the baseline smoke check):

# Compute Moran's I spatial autocorrelation on top SCT variable features (requires Rfast2 or ape).
spatial_data <- FindSpatiallyVariableFeatures(
  spatial_data,
  assay = "SCT",
  features = VariableFeatures(spatial_data)[1:1000],
  selection.method = "moransi"
)

SpatialFeaturePlot(spatial_data, features = top_svg, ncol = 2) &
  theme(legend.position = "right")

# Build the hexagonal Visium spot-adjacency graph (6 immediate neighbors per interior spot).
sq.gr.spatial_neighbors(adata, coord_type="grid", n_neighs=6, n_rings=1)

# Rank highly variable genes by Moran's I spatial autocorrelation and permutation FDR.
hvg_names = adata.var_names[adata.var["highly_variable"]].tolist()
sq.gr.spatial_autocorr(adata, mode="moran", genes=hvg_names, n_perms=100, n_jobs=1)
print(adata.uns["moranI"].head(10)[["I", "pval_norm_fdr_bh"]])

# Test permutation-based spatial neighborhood enrichment across expression clusters.
sq.gr.nhood_enrichment(adata, cluster_key="clusters")
sq.pl.nhood_enrichment(adata, cluster_key="clusters")

5. Interpret a pattern without overclaiming: Visium v1/v2 vs Visium HD and subcellular imaging

A feature appearing in a region supports a spatial association in this tissue section, not direct ligand-receptor signaling or lineage ancestry. Because nearby spots share microanatomical gradients and lateral mRNA diffusion during permeabilization ("spot bleeding"), spot-level Wilcoxon tests treating adjacent spots as independent observations severely inflate false positives. Match your interpretation and software stack to the physical resolution of the assay:

  • Conventional Visium v1/v2 (55 micrometre spot diameter, ~100 micrometre center-to-center): each spot captures roughly 1 to 10+ cells. In solid tumours, an invasive-margin spot routinely blends malignant cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts, and macrophages into one count vector; use spatial deconvolution tools such as RCTD (spacexr, Cable et al., 2022) or cell2location (Kleshchevnikov et al., 2022) with a matched single-cell reference rather than calling mixed spots "hybrid states".
  • Visium HD (2 micrometre capture squares binned to 8 micrometres or segmented into cells): increases observations from ~3,000 spots to hundreds of thousands of subcellular/single-cell bins, requiring disk-backed or sketched representations (Seurat v5 Load10X_Spatial(..., bin.size = c(8, 16)) with SketchData, or SpatialData / Zarr stores in Python; Marconato et al., 2024).
  • Targeted subcellular imaging (10x Xenium, NanoString CosMx, Vizgen MERFISH): records exact (x, y, z) coordinates of hundreds to thousands of targeted transcripts. Here the primary error source shifts from spot-level cell mixing to cell-segmentation spillover (assigning a T-cell membrane transcript to an abutting tumour nucleus when boundary masks are mis-expanded; run nuclear-only or Baysor / Proseg segmentation sensitivity checks).
Interpretation limit: do not treat expression intensity as a cell-type label or a causal signal. Review tissue integrity, library/slide identity, image registration, sequencing depth, spot-level QC, and the chosen assay before explaining a pattern. No universal QC cutoff or biological result is supplied here.

Practical check

For one conventional Visium library, record the input directory and versions using the commands above, run one language's loading and plotting fragments, and compare a library-size QC measure and an observed marker with the tissue image. Your check passes only when counts/features are nonempty, the image and spots are visibly aligned, and both color panels are interpretable; investigate the path, spatial metadata, image selection, feature name, or assay/layer if not. In a short note, state the coordinate/image choice, whether the pattern is qualitative or tested statistically, at least one plausible technical or composition-related alternative, and what additional evidence your interpretation would need.

These are compact workflow fragments, not a fully specified analysis: package versions, feature filtering, dimensionality choices, clustering resolution, and reproducibility settings need to be chosen and recorded for the dataset. A cluster boundary can reflect cell mixture, tissue composition, depth, or technical structure. Compare the map with morphology and QC before assigning a tissue-domain label.

4. Interpret a pattern without overclaiming

A feature appearing in a region supports a spatial association in this section. Co-location alone does not establish direct cell-cell interaction, lineage, or a causal tissue mechanism. Standard spot-level comparisons also need to account for dependence between nearby observations when making inferential claims. Spatially variable-gene methods and deconvolution address different questions; neither substitutes for checking their assumptions, reference compatibility, and uncertainty.

For spot-based assays such as conventional Visium, each observation can contain RNA from multiple cells. A region-level change may therefore arise from a shift in cell-type mixture, a within-cell expression change, or both. Deconvolution methods estimate mixture from a reference and add assumptions; their estimates are not direct cell counts. Imaging-based assays and newer Visium formats have different resolution and input contracts, so do not transfer spot-level interpretations automatically.

Interpretation limit: do not treat expression intensity as a cell-type label or a causal signal. Review tissue integrity, library/slide identity, image registration, sequencing depth, spot-level QC, and the chosen assay before explaining a pattern. No universal QC cutoff or biological result is supplied here.

Practical check

For one conventional Visium library, record the input directory and versions using the commands above, run one language's loading and plotting fragments, and compare a library-size QC measure and an observed marker with the tissue image. Your check passes only when counts/features are nonempty, the image and spots are visibly aligned, and both color panels are interpretable; investigate the path, spatial metadata, image selection, feature name, or assay/layer if not. Output: Python writes comparison.csv with retained sample counts, group means and standard deviations, treated-minus-control estimate, Welch statistic/degrees of freedom/p-value, a 95% confidence interval, and pooled-SD Cohen's d (note: pooled-SD Cohen's d assumes equal variances across groups, whereas Welch's interval and test allow unequal variances). Base R writes the same core estimate, interval, statistic, degrees of freedom, and p-value to comparison_R.csv.

Worked output and outlier sensitivity on the 8-unit fixture

Running Rscript --vanilla compare_groups.R data/control.csv data/treated.csv results on the 8-observation fixture above (executed locally on R 4.6.1) produces these exact summary numbers:

Control (n = 4): mean = 9.6500, SD = 0.6245   [8.9, 9.8, 10.4, 9.5]
Treated (n = 4): mean = 11.3500, SD = 0.5802  [11.2, 10.7, 12.1, 11.4]
Mean difference (treated - control) = +1.7000
95% Welch CI = [0.6557, 2.7443] | t = 3.9885 | df = 5.9679 | p = 0.007292

Read the interval in measurement units first: the observed treated-minus-control shift is +1.70 units, and values from +0.66 up to +2.74 units are compatible with the data at the 95% confidence level. Notice how fragile n = 4 per group is to a single aberrant measurement: if one control unit shifts from 10.4 to 14.2 (for example a mislabelled tube or haemolysed sample), the estimated difference drops to +0.75 and the 95% Welch confidence interval widens to [-3.0038, +4.5038] (p = 0.5864). Always plot individual biological units before trusting summary statistics, and investigate extreme values against wet-lab records rather than deleting points to rescue a p-value.

Inspect the data and interpret the comparison

  • Plot the raw observations by biological unit, alongside group summaries. With few samples, histograms and formal normality tests have little power to establish that a distribution is normal. Look for data-entry problems, severe skew, and influential observations, then check them against records instead of deleting them because they change a p-value.

library(Seurat) library(ggplot2) # Replace these directories with one directory per V(D)J sample (e.g. matched tumour and blood). sample_dirs <- c("data/patient1_tumour", "data/patient1_blood") sample_ids <- c("P1_tumour", "P1_blood") stopifnot(length(sample_dirs) == length(sample_ids)) contig_list <- lapply(sample_dirs, function(path) { loadContigs(input = path, format = "10X")[[1]] }) # Pass `samples` alone unless you need a separate secondary `ID` grouping. # Passing identical `samples` and `ID` vectors creates doubled prefixes (e.g. P1_tumour_P1_tumour_BARCODE). combined_tcr <- combineTCR( contig_list, samples = sample_ids, removeNA = FALSE, removeMulti = FALSE )

Each directory must contain Cell Ranger's filtered_contig_annotations.csv. Notice that combineTCR(..., samples = sample_ids) prepends P1_tumour_ or P1_blood_ to every 10x barcode; reserve the optional ID argument only when you want a two-part prefix such as samples = c("P1", "P1"), ID = c("tumour", "blood"). Before attaching contigs to RNA, compare head(combined_tcr[[1]]$barcode) against head(colnames(seurat_obj)); when merging separate per-sample Seurat objects, pass merge(s1, y = s2, add.cell.ids = sample_ids) so RNA and V(D)J barcodes follow the exact same prefix rule. Also document removeNA (single-chain cells missing alpha or beta, common due to TCR-alpha dropout) and removeMulti (cells with dual TCR-alpha rearrangements vs T-cell doublets).

Before comparing samples

Confirm that your RNA object's cell barcodes use the same sample-prefix convention as the combined contigs. Check which cells lack receptor calls, how many have multiple or incomplete chains, and whether the sample labels refer to the same biological units in both assays. A barcode mismatch can prevent annotation transfer.

2. Quantify clone-size bins, diversity, repertoire overlap, and V/J usage

Choose a clonotype definition before interpreting expansion. In current scRepertoire releases, cloneCall = "aa" groups paired CDR3 amino-acid sequences (which can merge convergent nucleotide rearrangements encoding the same peptide), whereas cloneCall = "strict" requires matching V/D/J/C gene segments plus CDR3 nucleotide sequence (preferable for tracking exact clonal ancestry between tumour and peripheral blood).

# 1. Relative clone-space homeostasis vs absolute cell-count bins.
# Note: scRepertoire v1 used `clone.call`; v2 uses `cloneCall`. Check `args(clonalHomeostasis)`.
clonalHomeostasis(
  combined_tcr,
  cloneCall = "strict",
  cloneSize = c(Rare = 1e-04, Small = 0.001, Medium = 0.01, Large = 0.1, Hyperexpanded = 1)
)

# 2. Clonal diversity across samples (Shannon weights richness + evenness; inv.simpson emphasizes dominant clones).
clonalDiversity(
  combined_tcr,
  cloneCall = "strict",
  group.by = "sample",
  n.boots = 100
)

# 3. Clonal sharing between compartments (e.g. tumour vs matched blood; Morisita-Horn accounts for abundance).
clonalOverlap(
  combined_tcr,
  cloneCall = "strict",
  method = "morisita"
)

# 4. Inspect TRBV / TRBJ gene usage skew before attributing expansion to one clone.
vizGenes(
  combined_tcr,
  x.axis = "TRBV",
  y.axis = "TRBJ",
  plot = "heatmap",
  scale = TRUE
)

By default, clonalHomeostasis() bins clones by their relative proportion of the sample repertoire. When one biopsy yields 250 T cells and another yields 4,000 T cells, a 3-cell clone represents 0.012 (Large) in the shallow biopsy but 0.00075 (Small) in the deep library. Whenever T-cell recovery varies substantially across samples, also inspect absolute cell-count bins in combineExpression(..., proportion = FALSE, cloneSize = c(Single = 1, Small = 5, Medium = 20, Large = 100, Hyperexpanded = 500)), and use downsampled bootstrap diversity (clonalDiversity(..., n.boots = 100)) alongside Morisita-Horn overlap (which is far less sensitive to under-sampled singletons than unweighted Jaccard overlap).

Depth and sampling affect the picture

Observed richness and rare-clone detection depend on sampling depth and cell recovery. Equalizing depth can be useful for a chosen comparison, but rarefaction is not a universal prerequisite or a cure for differences in tissue, capture, or library quality. Report the normalization or subsampling method and assess whether conclusions hold under reasonable alternatives. Do not label a large clone as antigen-specific from abundance alone.

3. Attach clone labels to Seurat metadata and map intratumoural phenotypes

Make the RNA object's barcodes and sample metadata agree with combined_tcr, attach clonal frequency bins, and inspect how expanded clones distribute across transcriptional T-cell states (for example CXCL13+ PDCD1+ HAVCR2+ exhausted vs TCF7+ IL7R+ progenitor/memory CD8+ T cells):

stopifnot(all(unique(as.character(seurat_obj$sample)) %in% sample_ids))

2. Compare clone-size structure

Choose a clonotype definition before interpreting an expansion plot. The example uses aa, amino-acid CDR3 calls. Amino-acid matching can group distinct nucleotide rearrangements that encode the same sequence; nucleotide-based definitions are more stringent for sequence identity. The package's available definitions and chain rules depend on current version and receptor type.

# Summarize the fraction of each repertoire in clone-size bins.
clonalHomeostasis(
  combined_tcr,
  clone.call = "aa",
  group.by = "sample"
)

# Show clone contribution by rank; this is a different view of abundance.
clonalProportion(
  combined_tcr,
  clone.call = "aa",
  group.by = "sample"
)

Homeostasis groups clones by their proportion of the selected repertoire; proportion plots rank clones into abundance groups. Neither is a diversity estimate by itself. Read the plot with its denominator and grouping in mind: the same clone may be assigned differently when the compared group changes. Record the clone-call definition, chain selection, grouping variable, and whether cells or reads underpin the input data.

In tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) cohorts, large clones frequently concentrate in cytotoxic effector-memory (GZMK+) and terminally exhausted (CXCL13+ PDCD1+) CD8+ clusters, yet viral bystander clones specific for EBV, CMV, or influenza can also expand inside human tumours without recognizing tumour neoantigens. Public specificity databases such as VDJdb (Goncharov et al., 2022) and McPAS-TCR are useful hypothesis screens, but CDR3-beta-only string matching without paired TCR-alpha sequence and patient HLA class I/II allele restriction carries substantial false-positive risk.

Interpreting clone-associated expression

A clone-size category is an abundance grouping, not a malignancy label. In a lymphoma study, determining whether a clone is malignant requires disease-specific evidence and study design beyond this repertoire workflow. A cell-level contrast such as FindMarkers() can be exploratory, but cells from the same donor are not independent biological replicates. For condition-level claims, account for between-sample variation, for example with an appropriate pseudobulk design, and validate findings independently.

TCRs and BCRs share V(D)J-based diversity but differ in chain organization and biology. The main code above is TCR-focused. For a real BCR analysis, use BCR-specific handling such as combineBCR() on filtered contig annotations and verify productive IGH plus IGK and/or IGL chains and CDR3 fields. For combineExpression(), choose a BCR-appropriate clone.call and chain (documented choices include IGH, IGL, and both); the scRepertoire documentation describes its heavy/light-chain handling and related-clone options. A heavy-chain-only call does not represent paired receptors. Check barcode overlap and resulting metadata before plotting. Interpret pairing and somatic hypermutation with BCR-specific methods. The small synthetic example below is a teaching summary, not a validated BCR pipeline.

Hypothetical decision check

Suppose an amino-acid CDR3 clone appears more prominent in a pooled treatment group than in a pooled comparison group. Before calling this condition-associated expansion, what definitions and units must you check?

Reasoned feedback

First state the clonotype rule, including chain handling and whether the display uses clone proportions or raw frequencies. Identify the denominator, for example receptor-bearing cells within each declared sample group, and check barcode/cell recovery. Then compare independent biological samples rather than treating pooled cells as replicates. Amino-acid matches can combine distinct nucleotide rearrangements, and abundance alone does not establish antigen specificity or function.

Exercise: audit a two-sample comparison

Run the workflow on two of your own samples. Save the two plots and write a short caption containing the four decisions above. Then inspect barcode overlap, receptor-call recovery, chain pairing, and sample-level replication before making a biological comparison.

Check your work: another analyst should be able to tell exactly how you defined a clone and what cells formed each denominator. A visually dominant category without that information is not an interpretable comparison.

Minimum cells per pseudobulk, paired donor designs, and apeglm shrinkage

Three practical extensions make sample-level pseudobulk workflows markedly more reliable on clinical and perturbation scRNA-seq cohorts (such as the public Kang et al., 2018 IFN-beta-stimulated vs control PBMC cohort from 8 matched lupus donors, GSE96583 / ifnb in SeuratData):

# 1) Audit and exclude ultra-sparse pseudobulks (e.g., < 20 cells of that lineage in a sample)
cells_per_pb <- table(as.character(meta_ct$sample_id))
keep_samples <- names(cells_per_pb)[cells_per_pb >= 20L]
pb_dense <- as.matrix(pb[, intersect(colnames(pb), keep_samples), drop = FALSE])
storage.mode(pb_dense) <- "integer"
coldata_sub <- coldata[colnames(pb_dense), , drop = FALSE]

# 2) Paired donor design (e.g., Kang et al. GSE96583: 8 donors measured in both ctrl and stim)
# Requires a 'donor' column in coldata_sub alongside 'condition' (ref = "ctrl"):
dds_paired <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = pb_dense[rowSums(pb_dense >= 10L) >= 4L, , drop = FALSE],
  colData   = transform(coldata_sub, donor = factor(donor), condition = relevel(factor(condition), "ctrl")),
  design    = ~ donor + condition
)
dds_paired <- DESeq(dds_paired)

# 3) Empirical-Bayes log2FC shrinkage (Zhu et al., 2019) for ranking, GSEA, and volcano/MA plots
# (keeps Wald p-values/padj while shrinking noisy low-count fold changes toward zero)
res_shrunk <- lfcShrink(dds_paired, coef = "condition_stim_vs_ctrl", type = "apeglm")

In Kang et al. (GSE96583) CD4+ T cells or CD14+ monocytes, accounting for inter-donor baseline differences via ~ donor + condition substantially sharpens precision over an unpaired ~ condition fit, surfacing canonical type-I interferon-stimulated genes (ISG15, IFI6, IFIT1, IFIT3, MX1, OAS1) at the top of res_shrunk while attenuating noisy single-UMI transcripts.

Successful structural check: output/pseudobulk/cd4_counts.csv has a gene column plus one column per retained sample, and sample_metadata.csv has one row per same sample with its condition. The DE results file has gene-level estimates; the plot files are written under output/plots/. Check that the count-column names and metadata sample IDs match exactly and that there is more than one independent sample per modeled condition. These checks establish file alignment and execution, not biological validity or a required direction/significance of effects. Stop if the sample mapping, count assay, or group labels fail; return to metadata and assay provenance rather than interpreting output.

Inspect sample variation and effect estimates

Use the variance-stabilized values to visualize sample relationships, not for DE testing. This PCA helps reveal dominant structure and possible outliers; separation by condition is not guaranteed or required, and overlap does not by itself invalidate the analysis.

GATK recommends splitting SNPs and INDELs before hard-filtering because annotation distributions differ by variant class (for example, INDELs tolerate higher FisherStrand values and lack meaningful RMSMappingQuality comparisons on many reads). Note that mixed multiallelic sites containing both a SNP and an INDEL are excluded by strict --select-type-to-include SNP/INDEL unless split beforehand with bcftools norm -m -both or handled with --select-type-to-include MIXED. VariantFiltration annotates records rather than deleting them, and FILTER=. is not equivalent to PASS. Preserve the merged annotated VCF for audit, then run the explicit PASS-only handoff below.

Germline versus somatic exome calling, and model-based alternatives

HaplotypeCaller assumes a diploid germline genotype model (expecting heterozygous VAFs around 0.5 and homozygous VAFs near 1.0); never use it to call somatic mutations in cancer exomes, where tumor purity, stromal admixture, aneuploidy, and subclonal architecture produce true somatic variants at VAFs of 0.02-0.30. For somatic WES, use gatk Mutect2 with a matched normal BAM (-I tumor.bam -I normal.bam -normal NORMAL_SM), a population allele-frequency resource (--germline-resource af-only-gnomad.hg38.vcf.gz), and a capture-kit-matched Panel of Normals (--panel-of-normals pon.vcf.gz), followed by GetPileupSummaries, CalculateContamination, and FilterMutectCalls. For single-sample germline WES/WGS, DeepVariant (Poplin et al., 2018; --model_type=WES) is also a widely benchmarked convolutional-network alternative that avoids manual hard-filter threshold tuning.

Success means the reports exist and parse, not that the sample passes assay QC. Check that FastQC reports correspond to both mates, flagstat has mapped reads, and the HsMetrics report contains target/coverage fields rather than an error or empty result. Many Picard/GATK releases require Picard-style .interval_list files (carrying the SAM sequence dictionary header) rather than raw BED files for CollectHsMetrics; convert your capture BED once with gatk BedToIntervalList -I refs/SureSelect_V6_intervals.bed -O refs/targets.interval_list -SD refs/GRCh38.dict and pass the resulting .interval_list to -BI (baits) and -TI (targets).

  • BAM-level QC: use samtools flagstat for alignment summaries and Picard CollectHsMetrics for PCT_SELECTED_BASES (on-target + near-target fraction), MEAN_TARGET_COVERAGE, FOLD_80_BASE_PENALTY (coverage uniformity), and PCT_TARGET_BASES_20X/30X. Interpret coverage against the assay design and validated callable-region criteria.
  • Variant counts and Ti/Tv reference ranges: in a typical human GRCh38 ~50 Mb coding exome, germline calling commonly yields roughly 20,000-30,000 PASS on-target SNVs (varying with ancestry, capture footprint, and padding) with a coding Ti/Tv ratio around 2.8-3.3 (higher than whole-genome ~2.0-2.1 because methylated CpG deamination enriches transitions in GC-rich exons while purifying selection removes non-synonymous transversions; random sequencing noise approaches 0.5). Use these ranges as cohort-level sanity checks rather than rigid pass/fail cutoffs.
  • Allele fractions: examine genotype, depth, allele-specific counts, mapping quality, and strand/read-position evidence together. Low fractions can arise from artifacts or biological mixtures; a histogram alone cannot distinguish them.
  • Per-variant evidence: inspect DP, AD, MQ, FS, and ReadPosRankSum when present, along with genotype and local read evidence. A fraction based on few reads is less stable than the same fraction supported by many reads; do not treat a fixed depth cutoff as a universal confidence rule.
